articles.title: Nous avons testé ce traceur GPS sur un bateau
articles.text:
Avec sa connexion 4G LTE-M, l'Invoxia Tracker GPS Pro Max suit les biens dans plusieurs pays et promet jusqu'à six mois d'autonomie. Nous l'avons embarqué sur un bateau pour tester ses fonctions de localisation et ses alertes au quotidien.
Après le Tracker GPS Classic Edition 2026, testé en 2025, nous retrouvons Invoxia avec un modèle qui voit plus loin. Le Pro Max reprend les fonctions de surveillance de son cousin, mais remplace les réseaux LoRa ou Sigfox par une connexion 4G LTE-M. Non seulement il permet des remontées de position plus fréquentes, mais on peut aussi suivre un bien dans plusieurs pays.
On retrouve le même principe d'un boîtier à glisser dans un véhicule ou un bagage. Sa carte SIM est intégrée et aucune démarche auprès d'un opérateur n'est nécessaire. Le GPS et le positionnement wifi servent à le localiser, tandis que le réseau mobile transmet les informations à l'application.
Invoxia annonce jusqu'à six mois d'autonomie avec une batterie de 2000 mAh et un suivi pouvant atteindre une position par seconde en mode direct. Bien entendu, l'autonomie dépend des réglages et de l'utilisation. Le Pro Max est proposé à 179 € avec un an d'abonnement inclus.
Le boîtier noir reste sobre avec des angles arrondis et une forme allongée. En main, la différence avec le modèle Classic est toutefois nette. Il s'avère un peu plus large et presque deux fois plus épais. Pour un appareil destiné à passer inaperçu, c'est une concession à prendre en compte.
La boîte contient un court câble USB-A vers USB-C et deux autocollants signalant une protection contre le vol.
La recharge s'effectue sur une extrémité du boîtier, où se trouvent également un bouton et un voyant.
L'autre côté comporte un passage pour glisser un lien (par ailleurs non fourni), sans pour autant faire office de fixation antivol sécurisée.
Le Pro Max reprend la certification IP67 du Classic, soit une protection contre la poussière et l'immersion temporaire. C'est un point particulièrement appréciable pour notre utilisation, puisqu'on a choisi de l'installer dans un bateau, où l'humidité fait intrinsèquement partie du décor.
Les habitués de l'application Invoxia GPS ne seront pas dépaysés. La mise en service commence par un branchement pour réveiller le traceur, puis un appairage avec le smartphone placé à proximité. L'assistant demande à quel usage l'appareil est destiné et si le véhicule est utilisé seul ou partagé.
L'app propose ensuite d'activer les alertes antivol. Elle indique que la présence du téléphone à portée permet au traceur de passer en économie d'énergie et de suspendre ces alertes. Il est aussi question d'un passage automatique en mode Perdu lorsqu'un mouvement est détecté en l'absence du smartphone afin de disposer d'informations de géolocalisation plus précises.
Les paramètres donnent accès à la fréquence des positions, aux notifications de vibration et d'orientation, à la sonnerie, ainsi qu'au radar de proximité. Le réglage standard prévoit un point toutes les 10 à 12 min. Choisir davantage de remontées permet de mieux détailler les déplacements, au prix d'une consommation d'énergie logiquement supérieure.
Trois modes sont proposés sur l'écran de suivi. Quotidien adapte les relevés à la fréquence choisie et aux mouvements avec une mise en veille à l'arrêt. Alerte abaisse les seuils de vibration et d'inclinaison pour signaler des mouvements plus légers. Absence privilégie une veille prolongée et l'envoi d'une notification lorsqu'un déplacement est confirmé. Les deux derniers sont temporaires et reviennent automatiquement au mode Quotidien à leur échéance.
Une fois configuré, le Pro Max fonctionne de façon très proche du Classic. L'application affiche la dernière position connue et les trajets enregistrés. Nous avons pu constater que le déplacement de notre bateau d'un port à l'autre avait bien été détecté.
Le traceur a également réussi à transmettre sa position au milieu du bassin d'Arcachon, alors que les antennes terrestres étaient éloignées. Une réception a priori comparable à celle d'un téléphone.
Les alertes de mouvement sont elles aussi arrivées. Sur un bateau à flot, leur interprétation demande toutefois un peu de recul, puisqu'un mouvement sur l'eau ne signifie pas forcément que l'embarcation quitte son emplacement. Une sensibilité élevée sera donc plus pertinente sur une voiture stationnée, dont on attend qu'elle reste strictement immobile. Pour le bateau, les zones virtuelles permettent de compléter la surveillance en demandant une notification à l'entrée ou sortie d'un périmètre.
La couverture internationale constitue un progrès majeur par rapport au Classic. La liste fournie comprend de nombreux pays européens, dont l'Allemagne, la Belgique, l'Espagne, le Portugal, les Pays-Bas et la Suisse. Un avantage pour garder le même traceur lors d'un déplacement à l'étranger, à condition de rester dans une zone couverte par le réseau LTE-M.
Il faut néanmoins vérifier sa destination avant de faire sa valise. Nous souhaitions initialement confier le Pro Max à un tiers pour un voyage au Vietnam, mais ce pays n'est pas pris en charge. Le Royaume-Uni fait lui aussi partie des exclusions indiquées dans la liste. La couverture est donc plus étendue que celle du Classic, sans être pour autant universelle.
Nous retrouvons les outils appréciés sur le Classic, comme le partage de localisation, le dossier de vol transmissible aux forces de l'ordre ou à l'assurance, et le radar Bluetooth pour rechercher le traceur une fois à proximité. L'app propose également de le faire sonner.
Ces services s'accompagnent toutefois d'un coût de connexion plus élevé. Après l'année incluse, le renouvellement du Pro Max revient à 59,95 €/an, contre 29,95 €/an pour le Classic au tarif actuel. La couverture internationale et le suivi plus fréquent nécessitent donc de débourser un peu plus.
Le Tracker GPS Pro Max étend son terrain de jeu grâce à la 4G LTE-M. Lors de notre essai, les déplacements ont bien été détectés et les positions transmises. L'app est complète avec des alertes réglables et des outils pratiques comme le radar de proximité, le partage de localisation et le dossier de vol. Le boîtier plus encombrant et l'abonnement plus coûteux demandent toutefois de bien évaluer ses besoins, d'autant que la couverture internationale n'est que partielle. Pour surveiller un véhicule ou un bien dans les pays pris en charge, le Pro Max est un allié efficace et simple à utiliser.
Le Tracker GPS Classic Edition 2026 constitue une alternative plus discrète et moins coûteuse à l'usage, tout en conservant plusieurs de ses caractéristiques. Il convient davantage à une surveillance dans le pays choisi à l'installation, sans avoir besoin de la couverture internationale ni du suivi plus fréquent du Pro Max.

articles.title: Corea del Sur dijo que Nvidia mantendrá el envío de 260.000 chips pese a la salida de Jensen Huang
articles.text:
El gobierno de Corea del Sur afirmó que Nvidia mantendrá su plan de enviar 260.000 chips de inteligencia artificial al país, un día después de que Jensen Huang renunciara como director ejecutivo de la empresa.
El viceprimer ministro y ministro de Ciencia y Tecnología, Bae Kyung-hoon, lo señaló en una publicación en Facebook. Según escribió, Nvidia reconfirmó que seguirá adelante con el suministro de las unidades de procesamiento gráfico (GPU, los chips que entrenan y ejecutan la IA) y con la cooperación con empresas coreanas.
La reunión fue presidida por el segundo viceministro de Ciencia y Tecnología. Nvidia anunció el 12 de noviembre que Huang dejaba sus cargos de presidente, director ejecutivo y miembro del directorio, y que la directora financiera, Colette Kress, asumiría como directora ejecutiva interina sin dejar su puesto anterior.
La salida de Huang se produjo tras el escándalo por su relación con una exejecutiva de la empresa Megaspeed, acusada de espiar para China.
Cómo se reparten los chips de Nvidia
El plan se anunció en octubre de 2025, durante la visita de Huang a Corea del Sur. Samsung Electronics, SK Group, Hyundai Motor Group y el gobierno recibirían 50.000 GPU cada uno. Naver Cloud, la nube de la mayor plataforma de internet del país, recibiría las 60.000 restantes.
De los 50.000 chips que le corresponden al gobierno, 35.000 se compran de forma directa y 15.000 a través del Centro Nacional de Computación de IA. Bae dijo que ya se aseguró capacidad equivalente a unas 21.000 GPU B200, un modelo de Nvidia, y que el resto llegará a comienzos de 2027.
Asimismo, Nvidia pagó 1,34 billones de wones (cerca de USD 1.000 millones) el 6 de noviembre por una ampliación de capital de Naver, con la que adquirió 4,13% de la empresa, según The Korea Times.
La cooperación incluye además conectar chips de IA coreanos con la plataforma de Nvidia mediante NVLink, una tecnología de conexión de alta velocidad, investigación conjunta en robots y máquinas con IA, formación de personal y la llegada a Corea de la conferencia GTC, el principal evento de desarrolladores de la compañía.
Por qué hay dudas sobre los acuerdos verbales
El empresario Elon Musk escribió en X el sábado que Huang “manejó la cadena de suministro de manera brillante”, pero que muchos de esos acuerdos “eran un apretón de manos con Jensen, no un contrato escrito”. Agregó que, sin él, “al menos algunos de esos acuerdos críticos se perderán”.
The Korea Times señaló que persisten las dudas, porque Huang habría dependido de compromisos verbales más que de contratos formales. El medio no identificó cuáles de los pactos con Corea se encuentran en esa situación, y ni el gobierno ni Nvidia lo precisaron.
El Comité Nacional de Estrategia de IA de Corea del Sur se reunió de urgencia para evaluar el efecto del cambio de dirección en la industria y en el suministro de chips, según la agencia Yonhap. El organismo dijo que el episodio muestra que la infraestructura nacional de IA no debe depender de la gestión de una sola empresa.
El comité planteó ampliar las opciones de capacidad de cómputo, incluidos los chips de IA fabricados en el país, y reforzar el intercambio de información con las empresas locales de semiconductores y de IA. Bae afirmó que el gobierno seguirá vigilando la oferta y la demanda de GPU.
El próximo hito concreto es la entrega de las unidades que faltan para completar los 35.000 chips de compra directa del gobierno, prevista para comienzos de 2027. El cumplimiento del cronograma previsto para 2027 será la próxima prueba de la continuidad de los acuerdos entre Nvidia y Corea del Sur.

articles.title: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry? | TechCrunch
articles.text:
We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.”
“Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.”
Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return.) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem.
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here.
Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days.
Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned.
But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down
Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia.
And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all.
Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about.
But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive.
So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key.
Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out.
Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago.
And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly.
But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more.
Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind.
I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America.
I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him.
Tim: I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang.
Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair.
Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the company has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups.
People talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions.
Rebecca: Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this?
Just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie.

articles.title: The new way to fight fires is with sound waves — 'infra-sonic' fire suppression system developed by former NASA engineers could kill blazes without water or foam
articles.text:
Forget water sprinklers — this 'infra-sonic' firefighting system from former NASA engineers promises to kill blazes using just sound waves
Sounds like a good idea
Fires are typically tackled using sprinkler systems and fire extinguishers across homes and larger buildings, but Ohio company Sonic Fire Tech is testing a fire-fighting system with a difference: it uses sound waves rather than water or chemicals.
The immediate benefits are obvious, in that people and properties don't get drenched at the same time as the fire is put out. There's another advantage too, because unlike water, sound waves can tackle grease fires — a type of blaze that's increasingly common.
Former NASA engineers form part of the team behind the "acoustic fire suppression technology", and Sonic Fire Tech raised $15 million in funding earlier this year, CNN reports. So is it the next big thing in fire defenses? These are the details.
How the technology works
The overall trend for fires in the US is, thankfully, downwards. However, while there are fewer fires than there were 40 years ago, they've become deadlier — if a fire is reported in your home, you're more likely to die. Fires from cooking have actually been on the rise in recent years, which is a worrying trend-within-a-trend.
As pointed out on the Sonic Fire Tech website, the standard dousing you get with a sprinkler system can cause as much damage as the fire itself in some cases: furniture and fittings get drenched, electronics are put out of action, and family heirlooms and keepsakes can be damaged beyond recovery.
With sound waves, those problems aren't there. In basic terms, the Sonic Fire Tech system works by producing high-pressure infrasound waves. These are sent down a dedicated system of pipes, in a similar way to how a sprinkler or air conditioning system would work, and then the sound waves are targeted at the source of the blaze.
The sound waves vibrate the oxygen molecules in the air, which essentially pushes them away faster than the fire can grab hold of them. That leaves the fire starved of the oxygen supply it needs, and it dies out. It can be put into action as soon as heat is detected, and false alarms don't matter, because there's no damage done.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
You can see how the setup might work in one of the official videos on the Sonic Fire Tech YouTube channel. In an apartment building, a network of ducting pipes lead from a central acoustic generator to each individual living space, with the emitters placed right over the cooking areas. Sensors detect the fire, and in response the sound waves are generated at the same time as the fuel supply for the cooking appliance is switched off.
The fire suppression tech has been proved to work at distances of up to 25 feet (7.6 meters), and certification testing is beginning before the end of the year — with the UL 300A protocol, for stovetop fire extinguishing, one of the safety standards that the sound wave system has been designed to comply with.
The challenges ahead
There's a lot that's promising about the systems Sonic Fire Tech is working on: there's nothing to run out of (only electricity is required), no water supply is needed (making this tech potentially transformative for wildfires), and there's no water damage or chemical residue when the fire's been put out.
It can tackle types of fires that water alone can't (grease fires), and it can act earlier and more reliably because false alarms are less of an issue. There's even a portable, backpack version of the system in development — one that firefighters could potentially carry with them when tackling blazes.
However, the technology isn't a sure thing yet, and there's work to do before you'll see it installed anywhere (or on board a fire truck). Researchers have actually been working on the idea of sound waves suppressing fires for several years now, and one of the challenges has been scaling the techniques up for larger fires across bigger areas.
There are also questions about everything that comes along with a blaze. "Sound may knock down a small flame, but it does not cool hot surfaces or wet fuel," Los Angeles fire protection engineer Nate Wittasek told Ars Technica. "That raises real questions about re-ignition, smoldering fires, hidden fires, and fires that are partially blocked by contents."
Michael Gollner, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at the University of California, Berkeley, has some concerns about whether the whole package will end up improving on sprinklers. "Water suppression sprinklers are terribly efficient, and this new technology still needs to prove that it’s more efficient than this," he told CNN.
These are challenges that the Sonic Fire Tech experts think they can overcome, not least because CEO and co-founder Geoff Bruder has a background in NASA, working on acoustic wave systems for spacecraft designed to land on Venus. That's a decent foundation for anyone working on putting out fires in homes and offices.

articles.title: FBI disrupts North Korean FaceStealer campaign behind $5 billion Binance hack — DoJ seizes FaceStealer cloud infrastructure containing 900 videos of tech workers, hackers used AI deepfakes to steal $400 million and compromise open-source software
articles.text:
FBI disrupts North Korean FaceStealer campaign behind $5 billion Binance hack — DoJ seizes FaceStealer cloud infrastructure containing 900 videos of tech workers, hackers used AI deepfakes to steal $400 million and compromise open-source software
The ongoing social-engineering campaign that's reportedly taken $400 million in cryptocurrency from victims and was behind the recent Binance heist now has a name: FaceStealer. The moniker came from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ), who have announced a fight against this crime wave, starting with the seizure of associated cloud infrastructure. According to the DoJ, North Korea is behind these attacks, stealing cryptocurrency to fund its government.
The DoJ's press release on the matter is blustery, but the FBI's detailed report contains the important details. The agency's techs seized "cloud-based infrastructure," containing 900 videos of targeted victims. FaceStealer is an advanced form of spear-phishing, complete with AI deepfakes, usage of the victims' contact networks and personal information, and carefully orchestrated preparation — sometimes months in advance.
The campaign isn't likely to stop despite the setback, and has reportedly been running for at least 18 months, a timeline that matches up with documented instances of similar intrusion attempts. The largest heist attributed to FaceStealer is the recent Binance hack that saw thieves make out the proverbial door with over $5 billion (most of it thankfully frozen and/or recovered), but far from the only one.
The FBI attributes about $400m in stolen cryptocurrency to the campaign, and importantly, also notes that the hackers have repeatedly tried to sneak into open-source software, chiefly Javascript/NPM modules and Rust crates. Despite not being mentioned by name, one example hack is almost certainly the Axios compromise from March 2026. The Node/Javascript library sees about 100 million downloads a week, and temporarily contained a remote-access tool — thankfully for only a few hours.
Jason Sayayman, the Axios developer in question, got hooked by an attacker posing as a legitimate company interested in hiring him. The malfeasants replicated the CEO's persona, created a Slack workspace with legitimate-looking channels, then invited him to a Teams meeting with multiple "people."
This modus operandi is what the FBI warns about. According to the bureau, FaceStealers start by getting access to a person's communication application(s), then lifting all previous conversations, contact lists, and, most importantly, stealthily recording video of them and/or their contacts. The footage and information will then be used to catch the actual targeted victim, who'll often be sent offers for jobs or investment opportunities.
The victim will eventually be invited to a Zoom or Teams meeting that's actually hosted on an attacker-controlled server, with a typo-squatted domain like "uu01webzoom.us" or "teams.livemeet.us". The meeting will often have deepfaked AI participants and/or previous meeting recordings playing, granting the event an air of legitimacy — particularly because conversations leading up to this point will contain real information and context.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
At some point, though, there will be some sort of "technical problem," and the victim will be prompted to install an "update" or software to fix the problem, which is loaded with malware. From there, the attackers have free rein over the victim's computer and data, and will siphon off browser sessions, CI/CD passwords, and all manners of access credentials to eventually get access to cryptocurrency wallets — or just use this information to find a juicier target, like the poor Binance developer through which Binance's hot wallets were broken into.
The FBI says that the above scenario may play out in multiple cycles until the attackers reach their intended target, collecting loads of precious video and information along the way to make the final strike much more convincing.

articles.title: Meta probó una app de predicciones donde se apuesta con puntos y no con dinero
articles.text:
Meta empezó a probar entre sus empleados una aplicación de mercados de predicciones llamada Takes, en la que los participantes apuestan sobre el resultado de preguntas o eventos con puntos y no con dinero real, según informó The Wall Street Journal.
Los puntos se llaman “cred”, abreviatura de credibilidad en inglés, según personas familiarizadas con el asunto citadas por el diario. La aplicación sigue en desarrollo, y el periódico señala que probarla con el personal es un paso que la empresa suele dar antes de un lanzamiento público.
Un mercado de predicciones es una plataforma donde los usuarios compran y venden posiciones sobre si un hecho ocurrirá, por ejemplo el resultado de una elección. Las más conocidas, Kalshi y Polymarket, funcionan con dinero real. Takes se distingue de ellas porque no admite apuestas de dinero, indicó el Journal.
Por ahora, la prueba se limita a empleados de Meta, según el Journal. The Block describió el funcionamiento como parecido al de los mercados que usan dinero: el acierto suma “cred” y el error lo resta, igual que en esas plataformas un acierto suma ganancias y un error implica una pérdida.
Entre las preguntas que circularon en la prueba figuró si el exdirector ejecutivo de Apple Tim Cook será el próximo director ejecutivo de Nvidia, según el resumen del reportaje que publicó Investing.com. La consulta llegó después de la salida de Jensen Huang de ese cargo.
El proyecto se conoció en junio con otro nombre
La aplicación continúa un proyecto del que se informó por primera vez en junio, cuando se llamaba Arena. Entonces se supo que el director ejecutivo de Meta, Mark Zuckerberg, había pedido a sus equipos construir una aplicación independiente de mercados de predicciones que usara puntos, según recordó el medio especializado The Block.
En aquel momento, Meta no había descartado permitir más adelante las apuestas con dinero real, según The Block. El reportaje del Journal no dice si esa posibilidad sigue abierta. La empresa declinó hacer comentarios.
Las plataformas con dinero real enfrentan demandas
Las plataformas que sí manejan dinero real afrontan demandas de estados de Estados Unidos que las acusan de ofrecer juegos de azar ilegales, según The Block. Kalshi y Polymarket sostienen que sus contratos sobre eventos son legales y que dependen de la jurisdicción del gobierno federal.
El 13 de noviembre, el presidente de la Comisión de Comercio de Futuros y Mercancías (CFTC), el regulador federal de los mercados de futuros, Michael Selig, criticó en la conferencia Cantor Convergence que los estados presenten cargos penales contra ejecutivos de estas plataformas. Dijo que las disputas deberían llegar a la Corte Suprema.
“Alguien dice que es juego de azar, alguien dice que es un derivado. Eso no es algo que deba poner a nadie en riesgo de ir a la cárcel”, afirmó Selig.

articles.title: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors
articles.text:
A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket lifts off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm local time Sunday. The rocket later suffered a failure.
Credit:
Manuel Mazzanti/NurPhoto via Getty Images
A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket lifts off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm local time Sunday. The rocket later suffered a failure.
Credit:
Manuel Mazzanti/NurPhoto via Getty Images
United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.
The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.
Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.
Sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC).
In a statement, ULA said the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.”
“ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the company said in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.”
Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible,” ULA said.
“ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.”
ULA’s Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 main engines made by Blue Origin.
Credit:
United Launch Alliance
ULA’s Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 main engines made by Blue Origin.
Credit:
United Launch Alliance
Something amiss
The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially said the anomaly occurred.
Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage issue was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem.
Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’s space company. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds.
Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance.
A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, showed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course.
ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The company then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin.
Amazon Leo’s launcher fleet. The Atlas V is no longer available.
Credit:
Amazon
Amazon Leo’s launcher fleet. The Atlas V is no longer available.
Credit:
Amazon
Wider impacts
Sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon.
First, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the company’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.
The Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the company has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity.
Amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers, not directly to consumers.
Previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the company planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.
“There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon said in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”
Amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’s Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan launches in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that company’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have launched so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.
Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but luckily for Amazon, the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.
What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.
That would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, Bezos’s chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9, and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.
It’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.
Vulcan’s earlier delays forced Space Force officials to move six national security launches from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA.
A US Space Force GPS navigation satellite is seen during encapsulation inside a Falcon 9 payload fairing. The eight newest GPS satellites all launched on SpaceX rockets.
Credit:
SpaceX
A US Space Force GPS navigation satellite is seen during encapsulation inside a Falcon 9 payload fairing. The eight newest GPS satellites all launched on SpaceX rockets.
Credit:
SpaceX
Expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.
But SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s company is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and new orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed plans yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years.
Amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 launches it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s New Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure.
NASA’s lunar program has another important link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently announced it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028.
“Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

articles.title: 357 detailed CPU die shots spanning 1971 to 2024 crammed into a new gallery — Motorola 68000, Intel 486DX2, AMD Athlon XP, Apple M1, and many more in beautiful detail
articles.text:
357 detailed CPU die shots spanning 1971 to 2024 crammed into a new gallery — Motorola 68000, Intel 486DX2, AMD Athlon XP, Apple M1, and many more in beautiful detail
Die shots were collated from masters such as Pauli Rautakorpi, ZeptoBars, John McMaster, and Fritzchens Fritz.
A CPU enthusiast has put together an eye-popping visual database containing crystal-clear, detailed die shots of 357 legendary and some lesser-known processors. At sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies, you will find a sortable, searchable, and filterable gallery featuring the outstanding, freely shared die shots from the likes of Pauli Rautakorpi, ZeptoBars, John McMaster, and Fritzchens Fritz. Find one or two of your favorites, and peer into the details to enjoy a nostalgic technological trip down memory lane. That’s what I did.
The unnamed collator of this gallery might not have contributed any die shots, but has still done an admirable job putting these macrographs and micrographs together in this way. Beneath a brief introduction that credits the skilled photographers who share these images for free, you can glide through the 357-photo collection.
By default, the die shot gallery gives you the gallery view, ordered by the oldest silicon first. Those browsing the gallery can instantly switch to a True Scale gallery view, too, which provides some physical sizing context. The next view option for the gallery is a table, where you can see processor maker, year, die dimensions, and photo license at a glance, but it sacrifices visual impact by showing just tiny thumbnails.
Navigating the gallery is also quick and intuitive thanks to a built-in search function. Using this, it was easy to display only 486 CPUs, for example. For your information, there are 17 486 CPU variants in this gallery with samples produced by AMD, Cyrix, IBM, TI, UMC, VLSI, and Intel of course. You can click any of the thumbnails to jump to a larger view with notes of the design, as well as photographer details/credits. Though that click zooms in the image considerably, I found that a right-click – open image in new tab - was needed to enjoy the die shot’s full visual splendor.
It would be great to see the database/gallery maintained with the latest shareable die shots from the various contributors. Also, it could be improved by fully populating details such as the die area, which is not always present. Some more searchable and sortable fields, such as transistor count, might also make this resource more satisfying.
For my personal nostalgia, I enjoyed seeing CPUs like the Motorola 68000 and the AMD Athlon XP up close. Surprisingly, some eras, including the Intel Ivy Bridge and Haswell generations, seemed underrepresented, though.

articles.title: Ola Electric hands the keys to dealers. What led to this shift in gears?
articles.text:
Ola Electric hands the keys to dealers. What led to this shift in gears?
For long, Ola Electric ran its own showrooms and sold directly to customers. Now it is shifting to a dealer-led model with plans to have 700 dealer stores by March 2027. What prompted this reset and what should the company get right for it to work?
On November 1, Ola Electric stopped taking orders at its own outlets. Most of them will be shut by December, as Ola moves away from the direct-to-consumer model that defined the company and turns to a dealer-led business.
Ola has recorded this in its investor presentation filed with the NSE and BSE on November 12 under Regulation 30 of the SEBI Listing Regulations. The document covers the unaudited standalone and consolidated results for the second quarter and half-year ended September 30, 2026.
In its Q2 FY27 shareholders' letter, dated November 12, the company calls the move towards a dealer-led model a "reset". What prompted this 'reset'?
The numbers tell part of the story. Consolidated revenue from operations was Rs 828 crore in Q1 FY26. It fell to Rs 690 crore in Q2, then Rs 470 crore in the next quarter, and bottomed out at Rs 265 crore in Q4 FY26.
Interestingly, the electric two-wheeler market has been growing in recent times. In Q2 FY27, industry volumes reached 5,99,317 units, up 82.7% year on year, and EV penetration in the two-wheeler market touched 11.2%. However, Ola's Q2 revenue fell 39% to Rs 421 crore in FY27.
The service record behind the reset
The shareholders' letter says little about why the direct model had to go, but public records give an indication.
The problems began with service. Between September 2023 and August 2024, the maker of electric two-wheelers received 10,644 complaints through the National Consumer Helpline. Of these, 3,389 concerned service delays and 1,899 were about delayed deliveries, according to media reports.
On October 7, 2024 the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) issued a show-cause notice giving the company 15 days to respond, and the complaints it cited included charges during the free service period, refusals or delays in warranty work, and unsatisfactory repairs.
Ola's response was that 99.1% of the complaints had been resolved to the customer's complete satisfaction. But the regulator reportedly found that 80% of those claimed resolutions had not been implemented, and the CCPA widened its inquiry.
Founder Bhavish Aggarwal promised the backlog would clear soon, and said the company would double its own service network to 1,000 centres by December 2024. Around the same time, a public spat erupted between Aggarwal and the comedian Kunal Kamra, who had taken up the customers' service complaints.
Subsequently, the company-owned store network ran into another problem. In March 2025, Bloomberg reported that only about 100 of Ola's roughly 3,400 showrooms displayed the trade certificate that the Motor Vehicles Act requires. Ola called the report misplaced and prejudiced.
Transport officials raided at least 26 stores in Maharashtra and six in Madhya Pradesh and impounded 60 scooters. Maharashtra's transport minister later said that of 432 showrooms inspected in April 2025, only 47 held valid certificates, and that the other 385 were shut.
The shareholders' letter does not connect any of this to the move towards a dealer network.
A new front end, built in eight weeks
The first set of dealer outlets became operational on September 4, on Janmashtami. By Diwali, on November 8, Ola says it had appointed 255 dealer partners operating 319 sales stores. The company is planning about 450 stores by December 2026 and 700 by March 2027.
Volumes through the new channel have climbed quickly. Wholesale orders were 3,955 vehicles in September and 13,505 in October. Ola expects 16,000 in November and 20,000 in December. Production is meant to keep pace, from 9,235 vehicles in August and 14,092 in October to about 25,000 in December.
The case Ola makes for dealers is financial as much as commercial. Under the old model, the company carried the stores, the stock, and the working capital. Now, it says, dealers pay for vehicles when they order and hold the inventory in their own showrooms.
Auto borrowings have fallen from Rs 2,422 crore in December 2024 to Rs 337 crore in September 2026, helped by a QIP and rights issue, and the company expects the auto business to generate free cash flow in the near term.
Operating expenses are meant to fall by a further Rs 50 crore as the company-owned showrooms close.
What the letter does not hide
The letter is candid in places. Inventory in the dealer channel built up through October and November, and registrations were a little slower in October. Ola puts channel inventory at about 15 days, and under a week in the earliest stores. It says that in markets where dealers opened early and have settled in, its market share is now well above pre-transition levels, though the company doe not give any figure.
There is also a supply problem. About 5,000 vehicles with paid orders in September were delayed by a week, running into October, because chargers were unavailable. The company says it is facing a paid order backlog and the constraint is its supply chain, not its plant, which it says can build well above the current output.
Hence the letter's headline claim: demand is no longer the constraint, supply is. The claim deserves attention. Wholesale figures count vehicles sent to dealers, not vehicles sold to riders, and the letter admits slower registrations in October.
The margin trade
Dealers do not come free. Ola says gross margin, which held at about 29.9% in Q2, will dip a little in Q3 and Q4 because of the dealer rollout, while operating margin should improve meaningfully. Excluding PLI incentives, Q2 gross margin was 26.5%. Gross margin per unit was roughly Rs 35,000, against an average selling price of about Rs 1,21,000, down from about Rs 1,68,000 in FY23.
The losses remain large. Operating EBITDA was a loss of Rs 218 crore in Q2FY27, wider than Rs 165 crore in Q1, and the loss after tax was Rs 362 crore. Consolidated free cash flow was negative Rs 371 crore, with the auto segment accounting for Rs 134 crore of that and the cell business most of the rest. Total borrowings are down from Rs 3,132 crore to Rs 1,819 crore.
The product roadmap
Going forward, Ola is betting on two things to win customers back: a cheaper scooter and its own batteries.
The cheaper scooter is the S1Z, which is expected to be delivered to customers by March 2027. It uses a battery type that Ola says costs less to build. The company plans to fit the same battery to its existing models. It also says that, as dealers open, demand will shift towards its premium scooters and motorcycles.
The batteries come from Ola’s own factory, which has reached its first 6 gigawatt-hours of capacity ahead of schedule. The government has extended a production incentive for the plant to 2031, and Ola expects the payments to kick in from January to March.
According to the company, making its own batteries costs the same as buying them, if about 70% of those made pass quality checks, and 10 to 15% less if 85% of them pass checks.
What to watch out for
A company not only owns its product but also owns every complaint that comes with it. While dealers will now share that responsibility, Ola cannot simply wish away all issues with a reset. It has to address the structural challenges that led to the bottlenecks and delays.
The success of the transition hinges on three major factors.
The first is sell-through: whether registrations keep pace with wholesale dispatches as the dealer network grows from 319 stores to 700. The second is supply: whether production really reaches 25,000 a month, and whether suppliers and chargers keep up with it. The third test is margin: whether the cost savings from closing company stores outweigh the gross margin given up to dealers.
Ola has moved quickly, and the early numbers seem to be favourable. But they are the company's own, and they cover only a few weeks. The real proof will come in the Q3 results.

articles.title: Google lance Gemini Finance : l’IA qui analyse vos comptes bancaires comme ChatGPT
articles.text:
Pour préparer les fêtes, Gemini propose aux Américains un budget établi d’après leurs achats de cadeaux et de voyages de l’an dernier, à partir des comptes bancaires reliés à Google Wallet. Google réserve ces fonctions financières aux États-Unis.
On vous en parlait déjà en septembre. Gemini retrouvait une carte d’embarquement et faisait le total des courses du mois dans Google Wallet, chez une partie des Américains seulement. Google officialise cette connexion et la déploie pour toute l’application Gemini aux États-Unis, sur le web, Android et iOS. Il ajoute Wallet aux applications que son assistant consulte grâce à Intelligence personnalisée, avec Gmail ou de Google Photos. Et pour analyser les dépenses, Gemini lit toujours l’historique des comptes et des cartes reliés à Wallet par l’intermédiaire de Plaid, une société américaine spécialisée dans la connexion bancaire.
Gemini repère les abonnements oubliés et les hausses de prix
Une fois la banque ou la carte de crédit reliée, Gemini signale les abonnements encore payés mais inutilisés, et les services qui ont augmenté leurs tarifs dans l’année. Il dessine aussi, dans la conversation, des graphiques des entrées et sorties d’argent, de la répartition des placements ou des budgets. Pour Noël, il propose un budget cadeaux et voyages calculé sur les dépenses de l’an dernier. L’utilisateur peut ensuite consulter, corriger ou supprimer les objectifs et les préférences financières retenus par l’assistant, depuis un résumé de sa mémoire dans les paramètres d’Intelligence personnalisée.
L’assistant ne déplace pas l’argent pour autant. « Gemini ne peut que lire les informations de vos comptes », souligne Google, qui lui interdit de payer avec les cartes enregistrées dans Wallet. Avec ces fonctions, Google répond aux outils financiers d’OpenAI, mais ChatGPT déclenche au contraire des achats au nom de ses abonnés chez les commerçants qui acceptent Visa.
Les transactions analysées par Gemini ne sont pas effacées automatiquement quand l’utilisateur déconnecte Wallet, d’après Android Headlines. Il doit effacer cet historique à la main, puis retirer les comptes reliés par Plaid dans les paramètres de Wallet pour couper le lien avec sa banque.
Google exclut l’Europe de son Intelligence personnalisée
Google déploie Intelligence personnalisée dans le monde entier, à l’exception de l’Espace économique européen, de la Suisse, du Royaume-Uni et du Nigeria, sans donner de raison pour l’Europe. Gemini Spark, l’agent IA personnel de Google, a lui aussi été ouvert à 160 pays, sans la France. En France, Google a activé la mémoire de Gemini, qui retient vos conversations passées, mais pas Intelligence personnalisée.
Dans Google Wallet, la connexion des banques par Plaid est en outre réservée aux utilisateurs américains. En Europe, la directive sur les services de paiement (DSP2) oblige tout service qui consulte vos comptes à obtenir un agrément auprès de l’autorité nationale. C’est pourquoi l’espace Finances de ChatGPT, lancé aux États-Unis avec 12 000 banques compatibles, ne lit les comptes d’aucune banque française. En France, Google Wallet vous sert donc à payer et à ranger vos cartes, mais Gemini n’analyse pas vos dépenses.
Si Google ouvrait un jour la fonction en France, le droit à l’effacement prévu par le RGPD vous permettrait de demander la suppression des transactions analysées par Gemini, une fois Wallet déconnecté.

articles.title: En 2010 vimos una avispa rara en este idílico pueblo de Navarra. Hoy las velutinas ya ocupan el 18% de la España peninsular
articles.text:
Es 5 de enero de 2019. De noche. Un equipo baja un nido de avispas asiáticas de un sauce blanco en Nigrán (Pontevedra). Está a 12 metros del suelo y en él vivían 1979 avispas velutinas, sin contar los huevos. Era una colonia en plena producción.
El único problema es que esa colonia debería de haber llevado semanas muerta: la velutina es un reloj. Los nidos se apagan entre noviembre y diciembre y solo las reinas pasan el invierno. En enero, en Pontevedra, esas avispas asiáticas no se habían ni enterado.
Y esto explica mejor que nada la forma en la que esta especie invasora se ha hecho con cada vez más zonas del país.
Baztán, 2010. La primera avispa asiática confirmada en España apareció en agosto de 2010 en Amaiur, en el valle navarro del Baztán. Quince años después, la cartografía del Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica la sitúa en unos 88.900 km², más del doble que en el periodo 2012–2018: en torno al 18% de la superficie peninsular.
No es, evidentemente, que las avispas tengan infectadas casi un 18% de la península. El Ministerio divide la geografía española en una cuadrícula de 10 × 10 kilómetros y, según su última cartografía, hay al menos un avispero de velutinas en 889 de esas cuadrículas.
¿Y sabemos cómo crecen? Sí, se están moviendo al este. El núcleo histórico de las velutinas está donde siempre, en el noroeste; pero si entramos en detalle, nos damos cuenta de que Cataluña y el Aragón oriental han pasado de 39 cuadrículas a 229. También hay puntos en Castellón.
Y el motivo de fondo, creen los expertos, es el calor. La dureza del invierno es una de las barreras que tenía a estas voraces avispas bajo control. Pero el frío está retrocediendo y, en esas circunstancias, los avisperos no paran ni un momento.
Se puede ver en esta cartografía: octubre de 2026 ha sido muy cálido en la España peninsular. Hablamos de 1,5 °C por encima de lo normal, el décimo más cálido de la serie. Pero hay un matiz clave: en el norte de Galicia y en zonas de Asturias y Cantabria, el núcleo histórico de la invasión, la anomalía rondó los cero grados. El calor ha aguantado sobre todo en el interior y el Mediterráneo, que es justo por donde avanza el frente.
¿Y ahora qué? Hoy por hoy, casi todo el esfuerzo se concentra en primavera y verano. Galicia capturó más de 230.000 reinas en 2025, y el 93% de las retiradas de nidos de ese año se hicieron en época estival. El problema es que la eficacia de esas trampas para reducir nidos no está demostrada y, en el proceso, caen muchos insectos autóctonos. Estamos cazando moscas a cañonazos.
Pero algo es algo. Y teniendo en cuenta su impacto en el medioambiente y el riesgo para la salud que conllevan, no podemos desperdiciar nada.
Imagen | Manuel Torres Garcia
En Xataka | Ya no hay forma de escapar del avispón asiático en España

articles.title: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
articles.text:
Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.
Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.
A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.
Untangling humans from the weather
Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.
Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.
Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.
The double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.
Sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.
A natural experiment in staying home
An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.
Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”
The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.
In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.
The results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.
Controlling for weather factors was important in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.
The 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.
Wang said, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”
Not every fire went quiet
In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.
There are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.
One line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires showed a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.
Mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.
When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.
This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.
Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.
Understanding the human Impact
Wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.
Wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

articles.title: SNL gathers all the tech tycoons for a lesson in dating and spycraft | TechCrunch
articles.text:
While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.
In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang.
Huang’s ouster from Nvidia (after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have serious implications for the tech industry; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league.
In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.”
Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about flights being halted all across the United States on Friday night.
“Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel said, leading to an obligatory mention of Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday. When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.”
“Look, I get it,” he said. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.”

articles.title: Was eigentlich hinter dem Protest gegen KI-Rechenzentren steckt – und warum Big Tech falsch liegt
articles.text:
Der große Irrglaube der KI-Firmen: Für Bürger geht es bei Rechenzentren nur um einen Aspekt
Als die Wähler:innen kürzlich in den USA an die Urnen gingen, war ich gerade in Ashburn, Virginia. Das Gebiet gehört zur sogenannten Data Center Alley und ist der weltweit größte Standort für Rechenzentren. Sie sind dort praktisch aneinandergereiht wie an einer Perlenschnur. Ironischerweise war dies aber auch der Startpunkt für die in Amerika stetig wachsende Gegenbewegung zu dieser KI-Infrastruktur.
Eine Fahrt durch die Gegend ist surreal. Entlang fast jeder Hauptstraße ragen monolithische Betongebäude empor. Sie tragen Namen wie Skybox oder CloudHQ. In der Big-Tech-Branche glaubt man, dass es bei der Bürgerbewegung gegen Rechenzentren um etwas Größeres geht als nur um die Rechenzentren selbst. Zwei Tage nach den Zwischenwahlen schrieb etwa Chris Lehane, seines Zeichens Chief Global Affairs Officer bei OpenAI, die Datacenter seien „zu einem Symbol für die öffentliche Unruhe“ geworden, wenn es um die Inflationskrise, Konzernmacht oder Kontrollverlust der Menschen über ihre Zukunft gehe. Mit anderen Worten: Es handelt sich um einen Kulturkampf.
