articles.title: China estrena su avión eléctrico por fin con gente a bordo, pero no revela lo más importante: la batería
articles.text:
China acaba de dar un paso de gigante hacia la aviación comercial eléctrica: la compañía aeronáutica estatal COMAC ha culminado con éxito el primer vuelo con tripulación de su avión comercial eléctrico, el CE-25A, del que hace tres años conocíamos su maqueta. Otros como el X1 de Heart Aerospace lo han logrado antes, pero ya sabemos cómo se las gasta China: ya domina en el segmento de los coches eléctricos y la gran maquinaria y ahora pretende hacer lo mismo con los vuelos. No obstante, lo más difícil está por llegar.
El hito. Este primer vuelo tripulado del CE-25A tuvo lugar el 14 de noviembre en Binzhou (Shandong) y en la aeronave viajaron tres personas: dos pilotos y un ingeniero de ensayos, según CGTN. Aunque el vuelo era autónomo, los pilotos supervisaban su comportamiento y podían intervenir en la cabina. Según los informes, la aeronave ejecutó la prueba con normalidad y cumplió con lo previsto.
El pasado dos de febrero realizó el primer vuelo sin tripulación y, tras 19 validaciones autónomas, según Air Data News, su prueba de fuego fue ayer. El avión estuvo en el aire 16 minutos y 38 segundos y en este tiempo recorrió 60,4 kilómetros.
Por qué importa. El primer vuelo tripulado del CE-25A con éxito es un check más dentro de su programa: permite evaluar el rendimiento del avión con persona a bordo y le acerca a su verdadero punto crítico: la certificación, tanto a escala nacional como internacional. De momento, las autoridades chinas ya han aceptado la solicitud y si el avión aspira a venderse fuera de China, también tendría que contar con el visto bueno de sus homólogos extranjeros.
Para ello es requisito indispensable que su batería cumpla ciertos requisitos técnicos, de alcance y de seguridad. Si lo consigue, podría convertirse en una alternativa al tradicional queroseno, al menos de forma progresiva y solo en algunos vuelos regionales, ya que esta tecnología todavía está verde en términos de calidad y precio.
El avión. El CE-25A es un avión comercial con peso máximo de despegue de 10 toneladas y capacidad para 19 personas. Según las cifras del COMAC recogidas por Interesting Engineering, tiene un alcance de 400 kilómetros, una velocidad de crucero de 300 kilómetros por hora y una altitud de crucero de 2400 metros, una configuración que lo aboca a vuelos de corta distancia entre ciudades.
Para la propulsión usa diez ventiladores eléctricos carenados integrados en el ala, cinco en cada lado, en lugar de las hélices convencionales. La gran incógnita es la batería: COMAC no ha revelado ni su capacidad ni el consumo. En cuanto a su nombre, COMAC explica que la "C" es por COMAC, "E" por ser eléctrico y el 25 denota el cumplimiento de las regulaciones para aeronaves de categoría de transporte CCAR-25 y la "A", porque es el primero.
Hay un viejo conocido detrás. El CE-25A es obra del COMAC pero no se entiende sin CATL, un viejo conocido en diferentes ámbitos y que sin ir más lejos, triunfa en el coche eléctrico. Colabora también la Universidad Jiao Tong de Shanghái, entre otros socios.
Esta alianza y objetivo viene de lejos: ya por 2024, el fundador de CATL Zeng Yuqun aseguraba que ya habían probado baterías en un avión civil de cuatro toneladas y que preparaban otro para 2027 o 2028 de cuatro toneladas y hasta 3.000 kilómetros de autonomía. Para ello, CATL prometía una densidad de 500 Wh/kg frente a los 200 Wh/kg de sus baterías actuales de iones de litio, un dato clave para la aeronáutica. Eso sí, no se refería a este avión en concreto, lo que denota que CATL tiene sus huevos puestos en varios nidos dentro de la aeronáutica.
Los retos. La ausencia de información sobre la batería es crítica y el proceso de certificación es largo y complejo. Y aunque sus datos estuvieran a la altura y eventualmente llegasen los aviones comerciales eléctricos y todo tipo de recorridos, el sector se enfrentaría a otra problemática: una flota eléctrica que cubriera todos los vuelos de hasta 741-1.111 kilómetros demandaría entre el 0,6 y el 1,7 % de la electricidad mundial de 2015, como calcula este estudio publicado en Nature Energy de 2018.

articles.title: Anatomy of a CPU
articles.text:
The CPU is often called the brains of a computer, and just like the human brain, it consists of several parts that work together to process information. Some take information in, some store it, some process it, and others send the results back out. In today's explainer, we'll go over the key elements that make up a CPU and how they all work together to power your computer.
This article is part of our Anatomy series, which dissects the tech behind every major PC component. If you want to go even deeper, our CPU Design series covers how processors are designed and built in much more technical detail. This article goes over some of those fundamentals at a higher level and brings them up to date with how modern CPUs actually work.
Compared to other articles in our Anatomy series (see the full list of hardware components below), this one will inevitably be more abstract.
When you're looking inside something like a power supply, you can clearly see the capacitors, transformers, and other components. That's simply not possible with a modern CPU since everything is so tiny and because chipmakers like Intel, AMD, Apple and Qualcomm only share their designs at a high level. The actual circuitry is proprietary, so the topics covered in this article represent the general features that all CPUs have.
It's also worth noting that what we call a "CPU" today is rarely just a CPU. Most modern processors are closer to a system-on-a-chip, packing integrated graphics, AI accelerators, memory controllers and more alongside the CPU cores.
It's also worth noting that what we call a "CPU" today is rarely just a CPU.
Every digital system needs some form of a Central Processing Unit. Fundamentally, a programmer writes code to do whatever their task is, and then a CPU executes that code to produce the intended result. The CPU is also connected to other parts of a system like memory and I/O to help keep it fed with the relevant data. Let's dive in...
The CPU Blueprint
When analyzing any CPU, the first thing you'll come across is the Instruction Set Architecture or ISA. This is the figurative blueprint for what a CPU can do and how software communicates with it. Just like there are many breeds of dogs within the same species, there are many different types of ISAs a CPU can be built on.
The two most common types are x86, which is most dominant in desktop PCs, laptops and servers, and Arm, which powers nearly every smartphone and has spread well beyond mobile. Apple moved the Mac to its own Arm chips in 2020, Qualcomm's Snapdragon X processors brought Arm to Windows, and Arm designs now run a growing share of cloud and AI server chips from Amazon, Nvidia and Google.
There are others too. RISC-V, an open and royalty-free ISA, has grown from a niche project into a serious contender. Billions of RISC-V cores already ship inside microcontrollers and the architecture is slowly pushing into PCs, servers and AI chips. Older ISAs like MIPS and PowerPC have faded into niche roles.
- An ISA specifies what instructions the CPU can process, which registers software can use, how memory is addressed, and more.
- How a chip actually carries out those instructions, including its pipeline, caches and execution units, is called the microarchitecture, and that's where chipmakers compete.
AMD's Zen 5 and Intel's Lion Cove cores both run the same x86 code, but they are built very differently inside. ISAs also keep evolving: Intel and AMD formed an x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group in 2024 to coordinate future extensions to the architecture.
To cover the main portions of a CPU, we'll follow the path an instruction takes as it is executed. Different types of instructions may follow different paths and use different parts of a CPU, but we'll generalize here to cover the biggest parts.
We'll start with the most basic design of a single-core processor and gradually add complexity as we get towards a more modern design.
Control Unit and Datapath
The parts of a CPU can be divided into two: the control unit and the datapath. Imagine a train. The engine is what moves the train, but the engineer is pulling the levers behind the scenes and controlling the different aspects of the engine. A CPU is the same way.
The datapath is like the engine and, as the name suggests, is the path where the data flows as it is processed. The datapath receives the inputs, processes them, and sends them out to the right place when they are done. The control unit tells the datapath how to operate, like the engineer driving the train. Depending on the instruction, the control unit will route signals to different components, turn on and off different parts of the datapath, and monitor the state of the CPU.
The Instruction Cycle: Fetch
The first thing our CPU must do is figure out what instructions to execute next and transfer them from memory into the CPU. Instructions are typically produced by a compiler and are specific to the CPU's ISA. ISAs will share most common types of instructions like load, store, add, subtract, etc., but there may be additional special types of instructions unique to each particular ISA. The control unit will know what signals need to be routed where for each type of instruction.
When you run a .exe on Windows, for example, the code for that program is moved into memory and the CPU is told what address the first instruction starts at. The CPU always maintains an internal register that holds the memory location of the next instruction to be executed. This is called the Program Counter (PC).
Once it knows where to start, the first step of the instruction cycle is to get that instruction. This moves the instruction from memory into the CPU's instruction register and is known as the Fetch stage. Realistically, the instruction is likely to be in the CPU's cache already, but we'll cover those details in a bit.
In practice, modern CPUs don't fetch one instruction at a time. They grab a block of dozens of bytes every cycle, which can hold several instructions at once. The fetch unit doesn't wait to be told where to go next either. A branch predictor, which we'll cover later, constantly guesses where the program is headed and steers fetching ahead of time so the rest of the CPU is never left waiting for work.
The Instruction Cycle: Decode
When the CPU has an instruction, it needs to figure out specifically what type of instruction it is. This is called the Decode stage. Each instruction will have a certain set of bits called the Opcode that tells the CPU how to interpret it. This is similar to how different file extensions are used to tell a computer how to interpret a file. For example, .jpg and .png are both image files, but they organize data in a different way so the computer needs to know the type in order to properly interpret them.
Depending on how complex the ISA is, the instruction decode portion of the CPU may get complex. RISC-V's base instruction set has only a few dozen instructions (optional extensions add more), while x86 has well over a thousand, many with multiple variants. x86 instructions also vary in length from 1 to 15 bytes, so the CPU has to work out where one instruction ends and the next begins before it can even decode them.
That makes decoding one of the most challenging parts of an x86 CPU from Intel or AMD, and one that takes up a lot of space. Arm instructions, by contrast, are a fixed 4 bytes, which is one reason Apple's cores can decode eight or more instructions per cycle.
To ease the burden, x86 CPUs break complex instructions down into simpler internal operations called micro-ops, and store recently decoded micro-ops in a dedicated micro-op cache.
When the same code runs again, which happens constantly in loops, the CPU can skip the decoders entirely. Intel has used this trick since Sandy Bridge in 2011, and AMD since the original Zen in 2017.
The most common types of instructions that a CPU would decode are memory, arithmetic or branch instructions.
3 Main Instruction Types
- A memory instruction may be something like "read the value from memory address 1234 into value A" or "write value B to memory address 5678."
- An arithmetic instruction might be something like "add value A to value B and store the result into value C."
- A branch instruction might be something like "execute this code if value C is positive or execute that code if value C is negative."
A typical program may chain these together to come up with something like "add the value at memory address 1234 to the value at memory address 5678 and store it in memory address 4321 if the result is positive or at address 8765 if the result is negative."
Before we start executing the instruction we just decoded, we need to pause for a moment to talk about registers... a CPU has a few very small but very fast pieces of memory called registers. On a 64-bit CPU, the general-purpose registers hold 64 bits each, and there are only a handful of them: 16 on x86 and 31 on Arm. CPUs also have wider vector registers, up to 512 bits each, used to process many values at once.
These are used to store values that are currently being used and can be thought of as the very top of the memory hierarchy (an "L0 cache" or sorts), even faster than the L1 cache. In the instruction examples above, values A, B, and C would all be stored in registers.
Those are the registers software can see. Behind the scenes, modern CPUs keep hundreds of physical registers and use a technique called register renaming to map them to the few that programs use.
This lets the CPU work on many instructions at once without them overwriting each other's values, which becomes important when we get to out-of-order execution.
Execute and the ALU
Back to the execution stage now. This will be different for the 3 types of instructions we talked about above, so we'll cover each one separately.
We'll start with arithmetic instructions since they are the easiest to understand. These types of instructions are fed into an Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) for processing. An ALU is a circuit that typically takes two inputs with a control signal and outputs a result.
Imagine a basic calculator you used in middle school. To perform an operation, you type in the two input numbers as well as what type of operation you want to perform. The calculator does the computation and outputs the result.
In the case of our CPU's ALU, the type of operation is determined by the instruction's opcode and the control unit would send that to the ALU. In addition to basic arithmetic, ALUs can also perform bitwise operations like AND, OR, NOT, and XOR. The ALU will also output some status info for the control unit about the calculation it has just completed. This could include things like whether the result was positive, negative, zero, or had an overflow.
That's a big part of why modern CPUs are so much faster than older ones running at similar clock speeds.
A modern CPU core doesn't have just one ALU. High-end designs have half a dozen or more integer ALUs working in parallel, plus separate units for floating-point math and vector instructions, which can apply the same operation to a whole batch of numbers at once. That's a big part of why modern CPUs are so much faster than older ones running at similar clock speeds.
An ALU is most associated with arithmetic operations, but it may also be used for memory or branch instructions. For example, the CPU may need to calculate a memory address given as the result of a previous arithmetic operation.
It may also need to calculate the offset to add to the program counter that a branch instruction requires. Something like "if the previous result was negative, jump ahead 20 instructions." In modern CPUs, memory address calculations are usually handed off to dedicated "AGUs" or Address Generation Units, but the principle is the same.
Memory and the Cache Hierarchy
For memory instructions, we'll need to understand a concept called the Memory Hierarchy. This represents the relationship between caches, RAM, and main storage.
When a CPU receives a memory instruction for a piece of data that it doesn't yet have locally in its registers, it will go down the memory hierarchy until it finds it. Most modern CPUs contain three levels of cache: L1, L2, and L3, and some recent designs add a fourth.
The first place the CPU will check is the L1 cache. This is the smallest and fastest level. The L1 cache is typically split into a portion for data and a portion for instructions. Remember, instructions need to be fetched from memory just like data.
A typical L1 cache is tiny, usually 32 to 64KB each for data and instructions per core. If the CPU can't find what it's looking for in the L1 cache, it will check the L2 cache. This is usually 1 to 3MB per core on current desktop chips.
The next step is the L3 cache, which may be a few tens of MB and is shared between cores. AMD's X3D chips stack an extra 64MB of L3 directly on top of the processor, which is why they're so strong in games, a workload that benefits greatly from more cache.
If the CPU can't find the data it needs in the L3 cache, it will go to RAM. If the data isn't in RAM either, the operating system has to load it from storage, which is far slower still. As we go down each step, the available space increases by roughly an order of magnitude, but so does the latency.
Once the CPU finds the data, it will bring it up the hierarchy so that the CPU has fast access to it if needed in the future. There are a lot of steps here, but it ensures that the CPU has fast access to the data it needs.
For example, the CPU can read from its internal registers in just a cycle or two, L1 in a handful of cycles, L2 in a dozen or more, and the L3 in a few dozen. Going out to RAM takes several hundred cycles, and fetching from an SSD takes hundreds of thousands. A hard drive can take millions.
Each core typically has its own private L1 and L2 caches, while the L3 is shared among a group of cores, such as the eight cores on one of AMD's Zen 5 chiplets. Intel's efficiency cores are an exception, sharing an L2 cache in clusters of four. We'll talk more about multi-core CPUs later in this article.
Branches, Pipelining and Prediction
The last of the three major instruction types is the branch instruction. Modern programs jump around all the time and a CPU will rarely ever execute more than a dozen contiguous instructions without a branch.
Branch instructions come from programming elements like if-statements, for-loops, function calls, and return-statements. These are all used to interrupt the program execution and switch to a different part of the code. There are also jump instructions, which are branch instructions that are always taken.
Conditional branches are especially tricky for a CPU since it may be executing multiple instructions at once and may not determine the outcome of a branch until after it has started on subsequent instructions.
In order to fully understand why this is an issue, we'll need to take another diversion and talk about pipelining. Each step in the instruction cycle may take a few cycles to complete. That means that while an instruction is being fetched, the ALU would otherwise be sitting idle. To maximize a CPU's efficiency, we overlap the stages of different instructions in a process called pipelining.
The classic way to understand this is through an analogy to doing laundry. You have two loads to do and washing and drying each take an hour. You could put the first load in the washer and then the dryer when it's done, and then start the second load. This would take four hours. However, if you divided the work and started the second load washing while the first load was drying, you could get both loads done in three hours.
The one-hour reduction scales with the number of loads you have and the number of washers and dryers. It still takes two hours to do an individual load, but the overlap increases the total throughput from 0.5 loads/hr to about 0.67 loads/hr, and with enough loads it approaches one load per hour.
CPUs use this same method to improve instruction throughput. A modern Arm or x86 core typically has somewhere between 10 and 20 pipeline stages. And because modern cores also handle several instructions per stage and execute them out of order, a high-end core can have hundreds of instructions in flight at any given moment. Each design is unique, but one sample division may be 4 cycles for fetch, 6 cycles for decode, 3 cycles for execute, and 7 cycles for writing back the results and retiring the instruction.
Back to branches, hopefully you can start to see the issue. If we don't know that an instruction is a branch until cycle 10, we will have already started executing 9 new instructions that may be invalid if the branch is taken. To get around this issue, CPUs have very complex structures called branch predictors.
Some even borrow techniques from machine learning, such as simple neural networks called perceptrons, to guess whether a branch will be taken or not. The intricacies of branch predictors are well beyond the scope of this article, but on a basic level, they track the status of previous branches to learn whether or not an upcoming branch is likely to be taken.
Modern branch predictors are right well over 95% of the time on typical code, and they work so far ahead that they often guess where a program is going before the branch instruction has even been decoded.
Once the result of the branch is known for sure (it's finished that stage of the pipeline), the program counter will be updated and the CPU will go on to execute the next instruction. If the branch was mispredicted, the CPU will throw out all the instructions after the branch that it mistakenly started to execute and start up again from the correct place.
With so many instructions in flight, each wrong guess wastes a lot of work, which is why chipmakers keep pouring transistors into better predictors.
Out-of-Order Execution
Now that we know how to execute the three most common types of instructions, let's take a look at some of the more advanced features of a CPU. Virtually all modern processors don't actually execute instructions in the order in which they are received.
A paradigm called out-of-order execution is used to minimize downtime while waiting for other instructions to finish.
If a CPU knows that an upcoming instruction requires data that won't be ready in time, it can switch the instruction order and bring in an independent instruction from later in the program while it waits. To keep this from breaking the program, the CPU tracks every instruction in a structure called the reorder buffer.
Instructions can finish in any order, but their results are only made final ("retired") in the original program order, so from the software's point of view, everything happened exactly as written. This is also where the register renaming we mentioned earlier pays off, letting independent instructions run side by side without stepping on each other's values. This instruction reordering is an extremely powerful tool, but it is far from the only trick CPUs use.
Another performance improving feature is called prefetching. If you were to time how long it takes for a random instruction to complete from start to finish, you'd find that the memory access takes up most of the time. A prefetcher is a unit in the CPU that watches the pattern of memory accesses and tries to predict what data the program will need next.
If a program is reading through memory in a predictable way, such as stepping through a large array, the prefetcher will reach out to RAM and pull that data into the cache before it's requested. Hence the name pre-fetch.
Speculative Execution and Security
Branch prediction and out-of-order execution have a side effect worth knowing about. When a CPU guesses which way a branch will go, it doesn't just fetch those instructions. It executes them speculatively and throws the results away if the guess was wrong. For decades, that was considered harmless.
That changed in 2018 with the disclosure of Spectre and Meltdown, two families of vulnerabilities that showed discarded speculative work still leaves traces behind, mainly in the cache. By carefully measuring how long memory accesses take, an attacker could infer data the CPU was never supposed to reveal, such as passwords or encryption keys from another program. Virtually every high-performance CPU from Intel, AMD and Arm was affected to some degree.
Meltdown has since been fixed in hardware, but Spectre-style attacks are a whole class of problems rather than a single bug, and new variants continue to surface every year.
Chipmakers now design their cores with these side channels in mind, and some of the software mitigations come with a performance cost. It's a good example of how the same features that make modern CPUs fast can also make them harder to secure.
Accelerators and AI
Another major feature now routinely included in CPUs is task-specific accelerators. These are circuits whose entire job is to perform one small task as fast as possible. This might include encryption, media encoding, or machine learning.
The CPU can do these things on its own, but it is vastly more efficient to have a unit dedicated to them. A great example of this is graphics. Surely the CPU can perform the computations needed for graphics processing, but having a dedicated unit for them (an integrated GPU) offers orders of magnitude better performance.
A big addition in recent years is the NPU, or Neural Processing Unit, a block built specifically to run AI workloads like live transcriptions or local language models while sipping power. NPUs went from virtually nonexistent in PCs to a near-standard feature in just a couple of years.
The CPU cores themselves have also gained more specialized hardware. Wide vector extensions like AVX-512 can crunch 16 numbers in a single instruction, and newer matrix extensions, such as Intel's AMX on server chips and Arm's SME found in Apple's M4, are designed specifically to accelerate AI math.
Dedicated media engines handle video encoding and decoding, including the AV1 codec, so recording or streaming barely touches the cores.
With the rise of accelerators, the CPU cores may only take up a fraction of the chip, especially in laptop processors where the GPU, NPU and media engines are all integrated alongside them.
Going Multicore
The last major feature to cover is how we can connect a bunch of individual CPUs together to form a multicore CPU. It's not as simple as just putting multiple copies of the single core design we talked about earlier. Just like there's no easy way to turn a single-threaded program into a multi-threaded program, the same concept applies to hardware. The issues come from dependence between the cores.
The cores don't each get their own path to RAM. Instead, they're linked by an on-chip interconnect, such as a ring or a mesh, that connects them to each other, to the shared L3 cache, and to the memory controllers.
With multiple entities operating on potentially the same pieces of data, issues like coherence and consistency must be resolved. If two cores were both processing instructions that used the same data, how do they know who has the right value? What if one core modified the data but it didn't reach the other core in time for it to execute? Since they have separate caches that may store overlapping data, complex algorithms and controllers must be used to remove these conflicts.
Typically, separate cores will process instruction streams from different threads. This helps reduce the dependence between cores. That's why if you check Task Manager, you'll often see a few cores working hard while the others are hardly working. Many programs still aren't designed for multithreading, or only split their work across a handful of threads. There may also be certain cases where it's more efficient to have one core do the work rather than pay the overhead penalties of trying to divide up the work.
Simultaneous Multithreading
Many CPUs also let a single core work on two threads at once, a technique called simultaneous multithreading (SMT), which Intel brands as Hyper-Threading. Since even the best out-of-order core can't keep all of its execution units busy all the time, a second thread can fill in the gaps.
It typically adds 10 to 30% more throughput in well-threaded workloads for very little extra die space. SMT has long been a staple of modern CPUs, but Intel recently dropped Hyper-Threading from the performance cores in its Lunar Lake and Arrow Lake chips, opting to spend that effort on making each core faster and more efficient instead. Apple and Qualcomm don't use SMT at all.
Hybrid Architectures
For years, every core in a desktop CPU was identical. That's no longer a given. Borrowing the idea from how smartphone chips work, many processors mix large and fast performance cores (usually referred to as P-cores) with smaller and more power-efficient cores (E-cores).
Some recent laptop chips add a third tier of low-power cores for light background tasks as well. Intel adopted this approach with Alder Lake in 2021, and Apple and Qualcomm do something similar. Meanwhile, AMD builds compact "c" versions of its Zen cores that trade peak clock speed for size and efficiency.
The catch is that the operating system needs to know which core is best for which job. Intel's Thread Director, for example, feeds hints to Windows about what each thread is doing, so a game lands on the P-cores while background updates are sent to the E-cores.
Chiplets and Tiles
The other big shift is in how CPUs are physically built. We wrote an entire technical explainer about the importance of chiplets a while back. The idea is that instead of making one large piece of silicon, both AMD and Intel now split their processors into smaller dies, which AMD calls chiplets and Intel calls tiles, and connect them inside the same package.
For example, a Ryzen 9 9950X combines two 8-core compute chiplets with a separate I/O die that handles memory, PCIe and USB.
Smaller dies are cheaper to make, since a single defect ruins less silicon, and each piece can be built on whatever manufacturing process suits it best. The trade-off is communication: data traveling between chiplets takes longer than data staying on one die, which is why software and schedulers sometimes need to keep related threads on the same chiplet.
Advanced packaging techniques like Intel's Foveros and AMD's 3D V-Cache go a step further by stacking dies on top of each other.
Physical Design: From Blueprint to Silicon
Most of this article has focused on the architectural design of a CPU since that's where most of the complexity is. However, this all needs to be created in the real world and that adds another level of complexity.
In order to synchronize all the components throughout the processor, a clock signal is used. Modern desktop processors typically run between 3GHz and 5GHz, with the fastest chips boosting to around 6GHz or more. That's a modest increase over the past decade, as most of the performance gains have come from elsewhere. At each of these cycles, the billions of transistors inside a chip are switching on and off.
Clocks are critical to ensure that as each stage of the pipeline advances, all the values show up at the right time. But clock speed alone doesn't determine how fast a CPU is.
Performance comes down to clock speed multiplied by how many instructions the core can complete per clock cycle (IPC). Everything we've covered, from wider decoders and multiple ALUs to bigger caches and better branch predictors, exists to raise IPC. That's why a modern core running at 5GHz is several times faster than one from a decade ago running at a similar speed.
Everything we've covered, from wider decoders and multiple ALUs to bigger caches and better branch predictors, exists to raise IPC.
Increasing the clock frequency through overclocking will make the chip faster, but will also increase power consumption and heat output. These days, CPUs handle most of that on their own. Boost algorithms constantly adjust clock speeds and voltages based on temperature, power draw and workload, pushing each chip close to its limits right out of the box and without any manual intervention. That leaves far less headroom for manual overclocking than there used to be.
Heat is a CPU's worst enemy, that part hasn't changed. Modern chips are designed to run hot, and they automatically throttle their clocks if they reach their temperature limit, typically around 95 to 105°C. Long-term damage comes from the combination of heat, voltage and current, which slowly wears down the microscopic transistors and wiring.
This is why desktop CPUs come with heat spreaders. The actual silicon dies of a CPU may only take up 20% of the surface area of a physical device. Increasing the footprint allows the heat to be spread more evenly to a heatsink. It also allows more contacts for interfacing with external components.
Modern desktop CPUs have well over a thousand electrical contacts on the back. AMD's AM5 socket uses 1,718 and Intel's LGA 1851 socket uses 1,851. Both now use the LGA design, where the CPU has flat pads and the pins are in the motherboard socket instead.
Laptop chips are soldered directly to the motherboard using a grid of tiny solder balls, often numbering well over a thousand as well. Regardless of the design, around half of them are devoted to power delivery and the rest are used for data. This includes communication with the RAM, chipset, storage, PCIe devices, and more.
With high-performance CPUs drawing upwards of 200 amps at full load, they need hundreds of contacts to spread out the current draw evenly. The contacts are usually gold plated to improve electrical conductivity. Different manufacturers use different arrangements of contacts throughout their many product lines.
The transistors themselves keep shrinking and changing shape, too. The latest manufacturing processes from TSMC and Intel are moving from FinFET transistors to gate-all-around designs, where the gate fully wraps the channel for better control and less leakage. Intel's 18A process, used in its Panther Lake chips, also introduces backside power delivery, which moves the power wiring to the back of the silicon wafer and leaves the front free for data signals. For a much deeper look at how chips are manufactured, check out Part 3 of our CPU design series.
Putting It All Together: Inside AMD's Zen 5
To wrap things up, we'll take a quick look at the design of a modern CPU core: AMD's Zen 5, found in the Ryzen 9000 series. AMD has published detailed diagrams of the core, and nearly every concept we've covered shows up in it.
Starting at the top, the branch predictor runs ahead of everything else, guessing where the program is headed and telling the front end which instructions to fetch. Those instructions come from a 32KB L1 instruction cache, with help from the TLB buffer, a small cache that remembers recent translations between the memory addresses a program uses and their actual physical locations in RAM.
From there, the instructions go through two separate decode clusters that work in parallel, each turning x86 instructions into micro-ops. Code that has run recently can skip decoding entirely and come straight out of the micro-op cache. Either way, up to eight micro-ops per cycle are passed along to the next stage.
This is where the out-of-order machinery takes over. The micro-ops go through register renaming and are entered into a 448-entry reorder buffer, which tracks every instruction. They then wait in schedulers until their input data is ready. The exact workings of these are a bit complex (think graduate-level university course), but they are what let the core pick the most timely instruction to execute next while keeping results in the correct order.
Once an instruction is ready, it's sent to one of the execution units. Zen 5 has six integer ALUs, four address generation units for memory operations, and a floating-point and vector unit that can process full 512-bit AVX-512 instructions. Memory operations are served by a 48KB L1 data cache, backed by a 1MB L2 cache per core and a 32MB L3 shared by all eight cores on the chiplet.
The output results will be stored, the instruction will be retired in program order, and the CPU is now ready to start on the next instruction. That's about it!
While this article was not meant to be a definitive guide to exactly how every CPU works, it should give you a good idea of their inner workings and complexities (!). Frankly, no one outside of Intel, AMD or Apple knows every detail of how their CPUs work. Each section of this article represents an entire field of research and development so the information presented here just scratches the surface.
Keep Reading
If you are interested in learning more about how the various components covered in this article are designed, check out Part 2 of our CPU design series. If you're more interested in learning how a CPU is physically made down to the transistor and silicon level, check out Part 3.

articles.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
articles.text:
AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
- Date:
- November 14, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
- Share:
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.
Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.
The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.
AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss
The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.
Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.
Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.
Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.
The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.
"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict
Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.
Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.
For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.
Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.
"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."
The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening
Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.
But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.
The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.
At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.
"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."
The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.
How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns
Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.
The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.
The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.
This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.
"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."
Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.
"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."
From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments
The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.
Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.
Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.
These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.
For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.
Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.
Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?
Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.
Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.
Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.
"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."

articles.title: Así son los SUV con tecnologia de masajes, calefacción y ventilación en ambas filas: adiós al cansancio en la vía
articles.text:
Los vehículos actuales incorporan tecnologías orientadas tanto a la seguridad como al confort de los ocupantes. Es el caso de los BAIC X55 y X7 REEV, dos SUV de rango extendido que integran asistentes de conducción, cámaras, sensores y funciones de comodidad en la cabina.
El BAIC X55 REEV y el BAIC X7 REEV cuentan con sistemas de asistencias a la conducción y una arquitectura de propulsión en la que las ruedas son movidas por motores eléctricos. En el X7, además, los asientos delanteros y traseros incluyen ventilación, calefacción y masajes.
Las funciones de seguridad y confort varían de acuerdo con cada modelo y versión.
Cuáles son las funciones de seguridad de estos carros
El BAIC X55 REEV, en su versión LV4, incorpora un paquete de asistencias avanzadas a la conducción con cámara frontal, radar frontal de onda milimétrica, cuatro cámaras de visión periférica, 12 sensores ultrasónicos y controlador de parqueo.
El sistema incluye Frenado Automático de Emergencia, Alerta de Colisión Frontal, Control de Crucero Adaptativo con función Stop & Go, asistente para congestiones de tráfico y crucero integrado.
Asimismo, dispone de Alerta de Salida de Carril, Asistente de Mantenimiento de Carril, Mantenimiento de Carril de Emergencia y Prevención de Salida de la Vía.
A estas herramientas se suman la detección de punto ciego, el asistente de luces altas, la cámara de visión de 360° y el Asistente de Parqueo Automático, disponible en la versión LV4.
El BAIC X7 REEV ofrece un conjunto de tecnologías de seguridad activa, pasiva y asistencias avanzadas a la conducción. Incorpora Frenado Automático de Emergencia, Alerta de Colisión Frontal, Control de Crucero Adaptativo, asistente para tráfico congestionado, alerta y mantenimiento de carril, detección de punto ciego y asistente de luces altas.
Además, cuenta con cámara panorámica de 360°, asistente de parqueo automático, control de descenso en pendientes, asistente de arranque en pendiente, freno de estacionamiento eléctrico con Auto Hold y monitoreo de presión de las llantas.
Cómo funciona la función de masajes en el carro
El BAIC X7 REEV incorpora funciones de masaje, ventilación y calefacción en cuatro asientos: los dos delanteros y los dos laterales de la segunda fila.
El asiento del conductor cuenta con ajuste eléctrico en seis posiciones y soporte lumbar, mientras que el del copiloto tiene una configuración tipo “gravedad cero”, con apoyo eléctrico para las piernas.
El sistema de masajes tiene ocho puntos de presión, tres modalidades —Ola, Cruzado y Pasarela— y tres niveles de intensidad.
De acuerdo con la coma, estas funciones se pueden gestionar desde la pantalla delantera del vehículo y mediante controles físicos ubicados en la parte posterior de la consola central.
La ventilación de los asientos puede reducir la temperatura de la superficie de 55 °C a menos de 36 °C en aproximadamente 10 minutos, según la ficha técnica de la marca. La calefacción, por su parte, permite elegir entre tres niveles de temperatura: 36, 39 y 42 °C.
Qué significa que sean un carro híbrido de rango extendido
La tecnología REEV, sigla de vehículo eléctrico de rango extendido, funciona de manera distinta a la de un híbrido convencional.
En los BAIC X55 REEV y X7 REEV, las ruedas son impulsadas exclusivamente por motores eléctricos, mientras que el motor de gasolina cumple la función de generar energía para alimentar el sistema y recargar la batería.
En el X55 REEV, el motor de gasolina de 1.5 litros actúa como generador y el vehículo utiliza un motor eléctrico de tracción delantera. Su autonomía combinada es de hasta 904 kilómetros, de acuerdo con el ciclo WLTC.
El X7 REEV utiliza dos motores eléctricos que entregan tracción integral 4WD, mientras que su motor de gasolina de 1.5 litros también opera únicamente como generador.
Este modelo registra una autonomía total de hasta 762 kilómetros bajo el ciclo WLTC y no necesita conectarse a un punto de carga para el funcionamiento de su batería de 1,83 kWh.

articles.title: Test du eufy Baby Monitor E21 : la 4K s’invite dans la chambre de bébé — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le marché du babyphone connecté se divise grosso modo en deux familles. D’un côté, les écrans dédiés qui marchent tout seuls mais affichent une image digne d’un caméscope de 2004. De l’autre, les caméras connectées qui filment très bien mais vous obligent à garder le smartphone sous l’oreiller. L’eufy E21 veut réconcilier tout le monde avec une caméra 4K motorisée, un écran parent de 5 pouces et une application en bonus.
Design : on dirait du Apple
Premier bon point avant même d’allumer quoi que ce soit : la boîte est généreuse et pensée pour des parents qui n’ont pas le temps. Toutes les instructions sont visibles dès l’ouverture, le couvercle faisant office de guide illustré en six étapes, et l’intérieur est rangé comme un tiroir d’Ikea bien monté. On y trouve l’écran parent, la caméra, une base de charge pour l’écran, deux adaptateurs secteur, trois câbles USB-C (1,5 m pour l’écran, 3 m pour la caméra, 1,5 m pour la base), un bras flexible pour fixer la caméra au-dessus du lit, une fixation murale et le sachet de vis qui va avec.
Le petit détail qui fait plaisir : chaque câble porte une étiquette avec une icône indiquant à quoi le brancher. Impossible de se tromper, même avec un bébé dans l’autre bras et quatre heures de sommeil au compteur. Les mêmes étiquettes rappellent au passage de garder les câbles à plus d’un mètre de l’enfant. Pas très glamour, mais franchement indispensable.
Le contenu complet : caméra, écran, base de charge, bras de lit, fixation murale, câbles et adaptateurs.
La caméra adopte une forme d’œuf couché, toute blanche, avec un large dôme noir qui abrite l’optique et une petite antenne à l’arrière. Elle passe inaperçue dans une chambre d’enfant, ce qui est exactement ce qu’on lui demande. Sa base se visse indifféremment sur le pied de table, le bras de lit ou la fixation murale.
Mais c’est en prenant l’écran parent en main qu’on comprend où eufy veut jouer. Les matériaux sont de très bonne qualité, l’assemblage est irréprochable, et l’interface est d’une fluidité qu’on n’attend pas d’un babyphone. Sincèrement, on a eu l’impression de déballer un produit Apple. Les commandes vont à l’essentiel : une croix directionnelle avec un bouton central (qui sert aussi de raccourci « Focus on Baby »), un bouton menu, un bouton retour, un bouton pour parler à bébé et un bouton zoom. Une antenne se déplie sur le côté pour la portée. Pas besoin de manuel, et c’est tant mieux, parce qu’on n’a plus le temps de lire grand-chose.
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le YUKA mini 2 500 passe à 599 € au lieu de 799 € ! Plug & Play, sans fil périmétrique à enterrer, zéro installation prise de tête. Bref, déballez, lancez, et dites adieu à la tonte !
Installation : simple, sauf le support de lit
L’appairage entre l’écran et la caméra se fait en quelques secondes : on allume la caméra (appui de 2 secondes), puis l’écran, et l’assistant fait le reste. L’application eufy Baby est facultative, et ça, c’est une vraie bonne nouvelle pour ceux qui ne veulent pas créer un compte de plus. Si on souhaite l’ajouter, il suffit de scanner le QR code sous la caméra. Un film collé sur l’écran demande de mettre à jour le firmware avant la première utilisation, mais pas de panique : l’opération prend une à deux minutes au maximum.
Le seul vrai bémol de ce test se trouve dans le support de lit. L’accroche manque de profondeur, ce qui limite les montants sur lesquels on peut la fixer solidement. Surtout, le bras flexible ne tient le poids de la caméra que s’il est monté dans le bon sens : mal orienté, il se tord et la caméra pique du nez. Rien de rédhibitoire une fois qu’on a compris le truc, mais on attendait mieux d’un produit aussi soigné par ailleurs.
Image : la 4K, ça change tout
C’est l’argument massue du E21, et il ne fait pas semblant. L’image est incroyablement nette, et même en poussant le zoom 8x au maximum, on voit parfaitement bien bébé, jusqu’au moindre détail. Grâce à la motorisation (330° à l’horizontale, 60° à la verticale), on recadre à distance sans se lever, ce qui est l’un des plus grands luxes de la parentalité moderne.
L’écran parent affiche en 720p, et on aurait pu craindre un décalage avec la promesse 4K. En pratique, sur une dalle de 5 pouces, le rendu est très très bon. Et pour profiter de la 4K dans toute sa splendeur, il suffit d’ouvrir l’application sur smartphone.
La nuit, la vision infrarouge prend le relais en noir et blanc. On entend un petit clic au moment de la bascule (le filtre infrarouge qui se déplace), puis la qualité reste très bonne, aussi bien sur l’écran parent que sur le téléphone. On distingue sans peine si bébé dort, s’agite ou fixe la caméra avec l’air de préparer un coup.
Son, détection et bruit blanc
Côté audio, eufy annonce une réduction de bruit active qui gomme environ 20 dB de bruit ambiant, et le micro s’avère très bon. Il détecte aussi bien les mouvements de bébé que ses petits bruits. Le bouton dédié permet de lui parler à distance, pratique pour un « chut chut » réconfortant sans débarquer dans la chambre. On mesure une latence d’environ 0,5 seconde entre la réalité et l’écran, ce qui est imperceptible au quotidien.
Le mode Focus est bluffant : une fois activé, la caméra suit bébé automatiquement quand il bouge dans son lit. Les bruits blancs, eux, sont très finement réglables, avec une minuterie qui permet par exemple de les couper au bout d’une heure. Enfin, la température de la chambre s’affiche en temps réel, et des alertes peuvent prévenir en cas de pleurs, de bruit fort ou de variation de température, avec cinq niveaux de sensibilité. Très pratique pour savoir s’il faut ajouter une couche de gigoteuse.
Connexion hybride et application
C’est là que le E21 se distingue vraiment. Par défaut, l’écran et la caméra communiquent en direct, sans passer par la box. Si le signal faiblit, la fonction Smart Connect bascule via le routeur Wi-Fi pour garder la liaison. Et ça marche : on a emmené le kit chez les grands-parents, et la liaison directe entre la caméra et l’écran a fonctionné immédiatement, sans rien reconfigurer ni se connecter au Wi-Fi de la maison.
L’application eufy Baby est très intuitive et gère plusieurs caméras, idéal si on a plusieurs enfants. Elle permet l’enregistrement continu, les captures, l’affichage en écran partagé et le partage d’accès avec cinq membres de la famille. Le tout sans abonnement imposé, ce qui mérite d’être souligné.
Filmer la chambre d’un enfant n’est pas anodin, et eufy l’a compris. Les flux sont chiffrés (RSA-1024 et AES-128), chaque enregistrement est protégé par une clé unique, et un bouton physique permet de couper complètement le Wi-Fi de la caméra. Dans ce mode, elle ne communique plus qu’avec l’écran parent, en local. Pour les plus soucieux de leur vie privée, c’est un argument de poids.
Autonomie : promesse tenue
Autre bonne idée : la caméra embarque une batterie de 5 000 mAh. eufy annonce environ 9 heures d’utilisation, ou 5,5 heures avec la vision nocturne active. Elle reste évidemment branchée la nuit au-dessus du lit, mais on peut la déplacer pour une sieste dans le salon sans chercher une prise.
L’écran parent tient pour sa part une douzaine d’heures écran allumé, et retrouve sa base de charge à chaque retour sur la table de nuit. Lors de notre test, les chiffres annoncés ont été respectés, de quoi tenir une nuit complète, même une très longue.
Prix et disponibilité
Le eufy Baby Monitor E21 est affiché à 249,99 € sur le site officiel d’eufy. Bonne nouvelle pour votre portefeuille de jeune parent (déjà bien entamé par les couches) : au moment où nous écrivons ces lignes, il est proposé à 187 € sur Amazon. À ce tarif, la 4K, la qualité de fabrication, le kit complet et l’absence d’abonnement en font une excellente affaire.

articles.title: Pourquoi les États-Unis ont cloué des avions au sol dans tout le pays pendant plus de quatre heures
articles.text:
Les équipes de L3Harris, prestataire de l’aviation civile américaine, remplaçaient des câbles en cuivre par de la fibre optique sur un site isolé. Après leur intervention, le réseau des contrôleurs aériens a été saturé, et plus aucun avion n’a pu décoller des États-Unis pendant plus de quatre heures.
Vendredi, peu avant 16 heures à New York, la FAA, l’Administration fédérale de l’aviation, a interdit tout décollage dans le pays, avant de lever cette interdiction nationale à 20 h 15. L’agence n’avait pris cette décision que deux fois depuis le début du siècle, le jour des attentats du 11 septembre 2001, puis en janvier 2023, après la panne de l’un de ses systèmes informatiques. Selon Cirium, société spécialisée dans les données aériennes, les compagnies ont annulé plus de 8 200 vols vendredi soir, et au moins 3 000 autres hier. Sean Duffy, le secrétaire aux Transports, a présenté samedi les premiers résultats de l’enquête, mais il ignore encore si L3Harris a commis une erreur ou installé un routeur défectueux.
La FAA a coupé deux connexions qui saturaient son réseau
Dans un premier temps, un porte-parole de la FAA a seulement évoqué des problèmes de communication dans plusieurs centres de contrôle, chargés de guider les avions entre les aéroports du pays. Les ingénieurs de l’agence ont cherché l’origine de l’instabilité du réseau. Comme l’explique Rebecca Guy, directrice technique par intérim de la FAA, « nous avons repéré deux points qui interrogeaient notre réseau à un rythme très élevé, un millier de connexions toutes les quatre à cinq secondes ». Les techniciens ont aussitôt désactivé ces deux points, le réseau s’est stabilisé, et la FAA cherche encore la cause exacte de la panne.
Vendredi soir, Markwayne Mullin, le secrétaire à la Sécurité intérieure, assurait n’avoir « pour l’instant aucune indication » d’un acte malveillant. Mais la veille, la FAA avait étendu à tout l’espace aérien américain SMART, un outil d’intelligence artificielle chargé de conseiller les contrôleurs pour désengorger le ciel. Interrogé sur un lien avec cette IA, Markwayne Mullin s’est contenté d’une plaisanterie sur l’acronyme « SI », pour « super intelligence », le nom que Donald Trump veut donner à ce système.
« Nous n’avons aucune preuve d’un acte malveillant, et aucune preuve d’un problème lié à l’IA », souligne Bryan Bedford, l’administrateur de la FAA. Quant au syndicat des contrôleurs aériens, il affirme n’avoir jamais été consulté pendant la conception de SMART.
Sean Duffy réclame des fonds pour remplacer le matériel de la FAA
Vendredi soir, Sean Duffy accusait un matériel vieillissant et surchargé. Samedi, il a relié la panne à une opération de modernisation. L3Harris, prestataire de longue date de la FAA, remplaçait des fils de cuivre par de la fibre optique, et après ces travaux, un système de communication indispensable aux contrôleurs a été surchargé par un routeur. Sean Duffy veut donc savoir si les techniciens de L3Harris ont mal installé l’équipement, ou si l’entreprise a fourni un routeur défectueux.
Les journalistes lui ont demandé pourquoi L3Harris intervenait un vendredi à 15 heures, et non au milieu de la nuit. Le ministre a répondu que la FAA bascule ses grands aéroports vers de nouveaux équipements la nuit, mais les sites isolés en journée. « Nous allons réévaluer le moment où nous faisons ces travaux », a-t-il promis.
De conférence de presse en conférence de presse, Sean Duffy répète que le Congrès doit débloquer plus d’argent pour moderniser les équipements de l’aviation. La FAA vient tout juste de commencer à retirer les disquettes du contrôle aérien. Et en janvier 2023, l’agence avait mis en cause un sous-traitant, accusé d’avoir effacé des fichiers par erreur dans le système à l’origine de la précédente interdiction de vol nationale.

articles.title: Elon Musk signs petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO — over 130,000 sign online petition, but not all Nvidians support Jensen's return
articles.text:
Elon Musk signs petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO — over 130,000 sign online petition, but not all Nvidians support Jensen's return
A lot of people are rooting for Jensen Huang's return.
A letter demanding the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO has been circulating online and has already garnered more than 91,000 signatures at the time of writing. Elon Musk said on X that he signed a petition, but it is unclear which one he has signed. At least one large online petition has circulated, with other big names supposedly among the signatories, ostensibly including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and several prominent shareholders, partners, and current and former Nvidia employees. However, the signatories on this petition apparently aren't verified. Regardless, this petition has gathered over 130,000 signatures.
However, not everyone is keen on bringing Jensen back; Nvidia Vice President for Applied Deep Learning Bryan Catanzaro said on X that an online letter purportedly circulated at Nvidia is fake, and he had no involvement and wouldn’t sign it if it were real. He also reiterated his support for Colette Kress, the newly appointed interim CEO who would run the company while the board looked for a suitable replacement for Jensen.
Jensen Huang’s fall was sudden and dramatic — he went from being one of the leading figures in the hardware needed to run AI to completely resigning from the company he built in under two weeks. It all started when U.S. intelligence sources claimed that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, apparently close to the former CEO, was passing information to Chinese intelligence. The company initially denied this story, saying, “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”
But a little over a week after that story, more news came out alleging that Jensen had an affair with the Megaspeed executive, forcing him to finally admit his relationship with the alleged spy. This led to a flurry of investigations by his own company’s board, the U.S. Congress, and the FBI. Just as things were already escalating, another alleged affair surfaced — this time with an Nvidia executive. Amid this whirlwind of scandals and rumors that Jensen would be ousted from the company, Elon Musk said it would be an honor to hire Jensen. Nvidia announced Jensen’s resignation just hours after Musk made the X post.
When do you start your Black Friday shopping?
Despite the nature of his departure, it seems that there is still widespread support for Jensen from Nvidia’s employees, with thousands reportedly rallying behind him and calling for his reinstatement in an internal forum. The Stand with Jensen petition isn’t directly related to Nvidia, but it echoes comments from people inside the company that the former CEO was removed without meaningful due process. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership,” the public letter said. “The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”
Jensen Huang’s larger-than-life persona will be difficult to replace, with the board considering candidates including Arm CEO Rene Haas and Apple Chief Hardware Officer Johny Srouji. It’s probably harder for interim CEO Colette Kress, who’s temporarily stepping into the position while the company is in the midst of massive turmoil, especially with the allegations that Huang was removed because of the mass smuggling of up to 1.5 million Nvidia AI GPUs, and who has the job of reporting its third-quarter results as CEO for the first time on November 17.

articles.title: Google turned to AMD Epyc, not its own Axion chips, to secure its first confidential TPU
articles.text:
Google turned to AMD Epyc, not its own Axion chips, to secure its first confidential TPU
The reason says a lot about where trust in AI hardware really lives
- Google's new TPU 8tx pairs TPU 8t silicon with 5th Gen AMD Epyc "Turin" hosts to deliver confidential AI inference
- The AI juggernaut passed over its own Axion CPU, which hosts the 8t and 8i, likely because its audited confidential stack is x86-only for now
- The confidential TPU joins a growing number of chips even as key security details remain unpublished, even as Google and Nvidia already offer confidential GPUs to cloud customers
Google has added two more systems to its eighth-generation TPU family, and the one built for confidential AI leverages a host processor Google didn't design.
The TPU 8tx, detailed alongside the dual-chip TPU 8i Max in a Google Cloud blog post, pairs Google's accelerator silicon with 5th Gen AMD Epyc CPUs.
AMD also announced that Epyc forms the host foundation for what both companies call the first cloud TPU system with hardware-enforced confidential computing.
The same chip with a new trust boundary in tow?
Google's April 2026 launch split its eighth generation hardware into the TPU 8t for training and the TPU 8i for inference. Google bills this as the first time it has introduced four TPU systems in one year, but as ServeTheHome points out, the two newcomers are system configurations built on existing chips rather than new designs.
As per Taiwanese outlet INSIDE, the 8tx inherits the 8t's 12.6 petaflops of FP4 compute and 216GB of HBM, but swaps in the lower-latency Boardfly network used by the 8i. Google claims up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty, and pitches the system at regulated enterprises and governments that want to fine-tune, distill, and train agents on private data without moving it between clusters.
AMD says Epyc handles orchestration, data preparation, and the high-throughput link to the accelerators. Its Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) works with the TPU to extend the protected environment out to the accelerators, checking each one's identity and security configuration before granting direct access to protected memory
Prompts, model weights, and intermediate data stay encrypted in host memory and in transit, according to AMD, with hardware isolation while the TPU runs. Google, for its part, described the result as "keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use."
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Skipping the homegrown solution?
Google hasn't directly said why it passed over Axion, the Neoverse V2-based chip it unveiled in 2024 as its first data center processor. Its own documentation offers a strong hint, however: Google's list of supported Confidential VM configurations runs entirely on AMD SEV and Intel TDX machines, with no Axion-based C4A or N4A instances, and states that TPUs can't currently be attached to Confidential VMs at all.
AMD's release adds that Google security experts have performed deep reviews of AMD's security processor firmware, and that SEV already underpins Google's Confidential VMs, Confidential GKE, Confidential Space, and confidential Spark and Dataflow services.
It could be argued here that confidential computing is only as credible as the years spent attacking it, and Google's audited chain of trust runs through x86. Building an equivalent on Axion would mean qualifying new hardware before shipping a product whose entire selling point is the "trust" it comes with, making it a moot point.
The move however is not a win for AMD's latest silicon; ServeTheHome reported that Google chose Turin to match the TPU 8t's PCIe Gen5 x16 interface, noting that a Gen6 host such as Venice would add no accelerator bandwidth, and tying the decision to Google's 2027 qualification schedule. Venice is AMD's 2nm flagship; the 8tx runs on a chip based on a family of CPUs that launched in October 2024.
Mark Lohmeyer, who runs AI and computing infrastructure at Google Cloud, told reporters that select customers will be able to deploy the 8tx in their own data centers, Data Center Knowledge reported, noting that Oracle recently said it will offer TPUs on its cloud. INSIDE quoted Lohmeyer arguing that the technology lowers the risk of physical operators reaching sensitive data, even in third-party facilities.
As TPUs spread beyond Google's own campuses, hardware attestation becomes the mechanism that lets a model owner place weights on hardware someone else runs. That interestingly puts AMD as a crucial part at the root of Google's off-campus trust offerings, a bigger role than the 8tx's niche positioning would initially suggest.
It also revives August's rumor: A SemiAnalysis client note reported by Tom's Hardware, said "Market chatter suggests [Google] is working with AMD on a TPU project in the v10 generation," possibly with CPU cores on the same package. The 8tx confirms neither claim as its Epyc chips sit in separate sockets, and nothing announced on November 9 involves AMD in accelerator design, but it does lend credence to potential future collaborations between the chip designer and the AI juggernaut.
The news saw AMD closing at $508.58 on November 9, up 13.26%, after trading as high as $515.18 on more than twice its recent average volume and while not all of it can be attributed to this particular development even as Oppenheimer's Rick Schafer upgraded AMD to Outperform with a $600 target, calling its server and data center success "undeniable", one could argue that it was a sizeable, if not the overwhelming catalyst in play that day.
The TPU 8tx arguably won't turn AMD's Epyc into a formidable TPU business overnight, and Google has left enough unpublished that its confidential computing claims deserve scrutiny once customers can test them.
However, one does need to account for the fact that when Google needed a host CPU to stake its first confidential TPU on, it picked AMD over its own chip, and that endorsement will outlast one day's share price increase as the latter aims to broaden its AI business even as its CEO recently branded the company as "Data center-first" entity even as PC sales continue to plummet.

Rahim Amir is a UAE-based tech writer who enjoys building PCs as much as he enjoys writing about them. He has been professionally writing about PC hardware since 2023, focusing on buyer’s guides, hardware reviews, and sponsored content and features related to tech.
Having built hundreds of gaming PCs and being an avid gamer in his spare time, Rahim tends to have stronger opinions about hardware than most. This is particularly on display when he gets his way with powerful, but minimalistic RGB builds even as Small Form Factor (SFF) PCs come a close second.
