articles.title: Rachelle Hampton won’t admit how long she spent charting the use of ‘murmur’ in Twilight
articles.text:
Rachelle Hampton is a writer and co-owner at Defector Media, and the host of Normal Gossip, a podcast of anonymous listener-submitted stories about everyday drama. Whether that’s lies about luxury wool in a literal knitting circle, the impeachment of a hypocritical HOA president, or a COVID outbreak at a destination wedding with an absurd 25 bridesmaids, each story is unique in its absurdity, yet weirdly relatable.
Rachelle Hampton won’t admit how long she spent charting the use of ‘murmur’ in Twilight
Normal Gossip host Rachelle Hampton is obsessed with I Like to Watch and splurges on good butter.
Rachelle Hampton won’t admit how long she spent charting the use of ‘murmur’ in Twilight
Normal Gossip host Rachelle Hampton is obsessed with I Like to Watch and splurges on good butter.
After years as one of the co-hosts of Slate’s In Case You Missed It, a podcast that required her to be chronically online, Hampton is enjoying being a little more unplugged these days. And she has perhaps the most interesting answer we’ve ever received to the question “what’s worth splurging on?”
What is your most indispensable tool (analog or digital, app or hardware)?
I think it has to be the Notes app. My entire life is in there! My relationship to the Notes app definitely changes depending on what’s going on in my life at the time. Sometimes I just use it to make my grocery lists, but there was also a period of time where I used it to house my weekly to-do list, so it was basically the only thing between me and destruction. I’ve started blog drafts in the Notes app, and I’ve used it to write out particularly fraught text messages. There are recipes I’ve developed in there, as well as passwords and also questions for my doctors. The first note in my phone is from 2018, so it also serves as a nearly decade-long journal, though there are definitely notes that I simply can’t decipher, like why do I have a note from July 2020 that just says “4th floor”?
Which is the most underappreciated?
I absolutely hate texting. (I write all day, I don’t want to do it in my free time!!) But as someone who also refuses to delete their texts, I have to acknowledge that my most significant personal archive is probably in my Messages inbox.
What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?
It’s a tie between Spotify and whatever phone game I’m currently addicted to, which for the last two years has been Township. I’ve never played Sims or Animal Crossing, but I’m told that it’s something like that. I just like planting my little crops.
How many tabs do you have open right now?
I maintain inbox zero across my entire digital life, so I close all my tabs after I finish a task. Right now I have three tabs that I will close immediately after finishing this questionnaire: the first is the Google Doc I’m typing in, the second is the landing page for this series, and the third is a Google tab where I just searched Animal Crossing to make sure I had the name right.
Which social media platform do you use the most?
It’s a tie between Reddit and YouTube. Hosting a twice-weekly podcast about the internet for three years either gave me some sort of PTSD or cured me of my social media addiction, depending on how you want to look at it. I can’t spend more than twenty minutes max on IG or X or Bluesky without feeling claustrophobic. The exception is when I’m sick, and I let my fever brain rot on IG reels. Otherwise, it just feels like too much information from too many different sources. Reddit and YouTube are both places where I feel somewhat in control of what I’m seeing.
What is your happy place online?
I don’t think I’ve ever been as happy online as I was on Tumblr between 2013 and 2016. I’m always subconsciously chasing that high.
What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?
My older brother bought me a tabletop Klipsch Bluetooth speaker for Christmas a couple of years ago, and it’s still going strong. The sound quality is incredible, and the design is super sexy, so it doesn’t immediately read as a Bluetooth speaker, which I love. I hope I never have to replace it.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
One of the stances I’m proudest of is that I’ve never (intentionally) used ChatGPT or Midjourney or any of the other generative AI tools / large language models. It’s getting harder and harder to avoid now that Gemini is built into Google and its various products. Stop trying to write my emails, Gemini!! I’ve never been swayed away from my belief that every single AI company owes a bankrupting amount of money to the writers and artists whose work their products are built on. Until that debt is paid, there’s nothing appealing to me about talking to a chatbot or creating a shitty poster.
What creation are you most proud of?
In 2020, when I was a staff writer at Slate, I spent a [redacted amount of time] methodically charting and ranking all 349 times Stephenie Meyer used the word murmur in her iconic Twilight saga. The idea had been germinating somewhere in the recesses of my brain for over a decade, only to be released by the surprise 2020 release of Midnight Sun. Seeing this blog come to life (shout out Slate’s interactive designer Natalie Matthews-Ramo!) felt like a fever dream come true.
What is your current obsession?
I’ve rewatched every episode of Netflix’s I Like to Watch with drag queens Trixie Mattel and Katya an embarrassing amount of times. There are certain episodes, like this one where Trixie and Katya react to Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, that I can quote front to back.
What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?
I wish I could say something chill and zen like take a cold shower or something, but the truth is when I’m writing and feeling stuck, I usually smoke a little weed, preferably a sativa strain. Getting high gets me out of my own way, which is usually the problem when I’m feeling stuck. It particularly helps with scriptwriting for Normal Gossip because the tone is so conversational, so being a little bit high stops me from over-writing.
When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?
My favorite coffee shop is less than 500 ft from my apartment, so I end up there without my phone at least once a week, either on purpose or by accident.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
Butter! With the caveat that I live by myself and don’t bake, so butter lasts a while in my household, but good butter can change a whole meal. It makes eating toast feel like a luxury instead of a chore to be completed between meetings because I’ve forgotten to eat lunch. My floor for butter is Kerrygold, but recently I’ve been loving this French brand called Isigny Sainte-Mère.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
Last to arrive, first to leave.
What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

articles.title: Can Indonesian researchers ever win a Nobel? Not without overhauling the research ecosystem
articles.text:
Will Indonesia ever win the Nobel Prize? That question probably pops into some Indonesians’ minds whenever Nobel season starts in October.
The reality is that there are no shortcuts to a Nobel. Breakthroughs recognised by the committee almost always stem from foundational work done decades earlier — often when it is impossible to foresee the practical payoffs.
Take the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded to Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth for pioneering optogenetics — a breakthrough technique that uses light to control nerve cell activity.
Read more: Bagaimana alga mengantarkan ilmuwan pada Nobel Kedokteran dan cara baru memahami otak
Interestingly, the road to optogenetics began with research that seemed to have nothing to do with medicine. Hegemann was initially investigating how the single-celled green alga Chlamydomonas swims towards light. His collaboration with Nagel eventually led to the discovery of channelrhodopsin — a light-sensitive protein that acts as an ion channel.
By 2005, Deisseroth’s team showed that channelrhodopsin could be harnessed to control neuronal firing with light. What began as a humble inquiry into pond algae laid the groundwork for optogenetics — now an indispensable tool for mapping and manipulating the brain.
This trajectory illustrates the road to the prestigious award: Nobel-worthy breakthroughs emerge from ecosystems patient enough to let basic research mature before demanding immediate benefits.
But can Indonesia’s research ecosystem nurture that kind of long game?
It all comes down to funding. Again.
The most glaring bottleneck in Indonesia’s research ecosystem is funding. The country’s R&D spending remains low, lagging far behind its ASEAN peers.
Data from the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) paint a sobering picture: in 2024, Indonesia’s total R&D expenditure stood at around US$2.8 billion — a meagre 0.23% of gross domestic product (GDP). Higher education shouldered 71.02% of that spending, while the private sector contributed a negligible 14.96%.
Neighbours tell a different story: the private sector drove 51.37% of R&D in Malaysia (2022) and roughly 74% in Thailand (2021). The lesson is structural: a nation’s scientific muscle depends not just on how much it spends, but on who funds it.
How should public research funds be accounted for?
Researchers must naturally account for every public fund they spend: explaining what they investigate, how funds are allocated and what discoveries emerge. Yet not all grant systems in Indonesia define “results” the same way — and rigid metrics can easily distort scientific work.
Take Indonesia’s 2025 Research and Community Service Guidelines. Under the Regular Fundamental Research scheme (PFR), grantees are mandated to publish at least one paper in a reputable international journal every single year.
Research benchmarks are indeed necessary. But when success hinges on short-term milestones — like annual publication quotas — scientists are almost guaranteed to play it safe, pursuing predictable findings over ambitious, high-risk discoveries.
Take Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who jointly won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work that began more than two decades earlier.
In 2005, the pair made a critical breakthrough: modifying mRNA’s nucleosides could suppress harmful inflammatory responses to synthetic mRNA. After years of funding rejections, skepticism and painstaking refinement, that fundamental discovery unlocked the mRNA vaccines and therapies that ultimately saved millions of lives during the COVID-19 pandemic.
By comparison, Japan’s Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research program, known as KAKENHI, still demands strict accountability: recipients must report on expenditure, track ongoing milestones, and submit comprehensive final evaluations.
KAKENHI explicitly urges researchers to disseminate their findings globally — via peer-reviewed journals, international partnerships, and academic conferences. Crucially, the guidelines avoid treating rigid publication targets as make-or-break funding criteria.
Lessons from Asia’s research ecosystems
In 2025, China boosted its R&D spending to roughly 2.8% of GDP. Its investment in basic research surged by 13.3% year-on-year – comfortably outstripping its 8.2% overall growth in R&D expenditure.
Meanwhile, Singapore committed S$S37 billion (around US$28.77 billion) to its Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 (RIE2030) plan. The blueprint balances market-driven applications with solid backing for open-ended fundamental science and homegrown scientific talent.
Both countries operate under distinct economic realities and strategic priorities. Yet they share a common thread: fundamental science remains an indispensable pillar of their national policy.
Boosting Indonesia’s research budget is crucial, but cash alone will not fix the system without deeper industry involvement and long-term backing for university laboratories. Accountability matters, too – but evaluation frameworks must be flexible enough to give unorthodox, exploratory ideas room to breathe.
Read more: Ribuan riset dan paten Indonesia terjebak di “jurang maut” karena tak dipakai industri
After all, scientific inquiry is inherently unpredictable. Hypotheses fall flat, experiments fail and dead ends are part of the process. A project that yields no marketable innovation within five years may still unearth foundational knowledge that sparks a breakthrough decades later.
Grant systems must therefore make room for rigorous science whose outcomes cannot be mapped in advance. Such work still demands robust evaluation – just not through the same narrow, transactional metrics applied to off-the-shelf product development.
The Nobel is a byproduct, not the destination
Indonesia does not need a glitzy roadmap to a Nobel Prize; it needs a dependable research ecosystem. That means reliable funding, smarter resource allocation, sensible evaluation metrics and real avenues for international collaboration.
Read more: Bukan (hanya) soal anggaran. Bagaimana dana riset dibelanjakan juga penting
Every nation dreams of its own Nobel laureate, and Indonesia is no exception. But the medal itself cannot be the end goal.
For Indonesia, the real debate is not a false choice between applied projects with immediate payoffs and curiosity-driven basic science. The challenge is designing an ecosystem flexible enough to nurture both, knowing full well that groundbreaking research runs on its own clock.
What matters far more is fostering a research ecosystem that empowers scientists to pursue bold, open-ended questions – even when the tangible payoffs are years or decades down the line.

articles.title: Où s’arrêtera BYD ? La marque chinoise veut maintenant concurrencer Smart avec une micro citadine électrique
articles.text:
Les hypercars explosant les 500 km/h et les limousines inondées de cuir ne suffisent visiblement pas à étancher la soif de BYD. Aussi impressionnantes soient-elles, les Yangwang U9 Xtreme et Altior risquent de se faire prochainement voler la vedette par une inédite micro citadine, placée tout en bas de la gamme. Plus petite que la Dolphin Surf et plus riquiqui encore que la kei-car Racco, cela existe ? Très bientôt, visiblement.
C’est en tout cas vers quoi convergent les derniers brevets déposés par la marque… Cette dernière travaillerait activement sur une nouvelle micro citadine avec deux portes et deux places évoquant furieusement la Smart #2. Aucune information officielle ne confirme cependant l’avancée réelle du projet. Il pourrait aussi bien s’agir d’un véhicule bientôt finalisé que d’une simple étude de style qui ne verra jamais le jour.
Des brevets révèlent un look façon concept-car, mais peu pratique
Cela dit, les images rendues publiques par l’Administration nationale chinoise de la propriété intellectuelle sont plutôt prometteuses. Le petit pot de yaourt présente ainsi une face avant souriante avec des feux reliés par un bandeau et un pare-chocs déporté en partie inférieure. Les roues semblent littéralement encastrées dans la carrosserie, ce qui donne immanquablement un aspect concept car à l’engin.
Mais ce design filant risque aussi d’impacter lourdement la polyvalence du véhicule. Comment en effet ne pas frotter les soubassements au moindre dos d’âne ? Un remaniement est à prévoir à ce niveau-là, si la voiture est véritablement confirmée. Là où la logique d’économie s’exprime à plein régime, c’est à l’arrière, au style parfaitement identique à l’avant. Cette stratégie très maligne rappelle forcément la Citroën Ami.
Face aux 290 km d’autonomie de la Smart #2, la barre est haute
La cible toute désignée, elle, restera bien la Smart #2. Et la chinoise aura fort à faire pour convaincre car l’allemande vise juste sur de nombreux points. Offrir jusqu’à 290 km d’autonomie dans un gabarit de 2,75 mètres relève par exemple de l’exploit. Bénéficier d’une puissance de charge de 65 kW en courant continu DC pour passer de 10 à 80 % de batterie en seulement 20 minutes est bluffant sur le segment.
BYD est largement capable de proposer des chiffres semblables. Seulement, osera-t-il vendre cet hypothétique véhicule en Europe ? Vu que le constructeur s’effondre en Chine, toutes les mesures sont bonnes pour gratter des ventes. L’arrivée du Racco étant de plus en plus probable chez nous, il ne serait pas du tout étonnant que cet engin lilliputien fasse aussi une incursion sur notre marché. Reste maintenant à savoir quand…

articles.title: TikTok tiene que cambiar: ante el abuso, no vale el silencio
articles.text:
TikTok tiene que cambiar: ante el abuso, no vale el silencio
Lo que nos preocupa a todos es que nuestra infancia esté expuesta, por la inacción de la compañía, a miles de pederastas de todo el mundo
Ante un problema sistémico no valen parches. Ante el abuso y el acoso infantil no vale con el silencio. Después de una semana publicando cómo TikTok no detecta el material de abuso sexual infantil explícito en abierto en su plataforma, la hipersexualización de menores, la recomendación constante de canales de venta de material de abuso, el trapicheo pederasta en los comentarios, directos de menores acosadas por hombres adultos… TikTok no ha ofrecido soluciones, más allá de remiendos y excusas. Tampoco ha dado la cara.
Esta es la tercera investigación que la Fundación Maldita.es hace sobre pederastia en TikTok. En anteriores ocasiones compartimos toda la información con la compañía, incluida una base de datos con más de 1.300 cuentas de pedófilos, y mantuvimos varias reuniones con sus equipos con la esperanza de que solucionaran el problema. Seis meses después hemos comprobado que, lejos de haber llevado a cabo cambios significativos, lo que nos hemos encontrado es aún peor. Lo que “TikTok, el hogar del pederasta” demuestra es un fracaso sistémico de la red social más utilizada por los menores en lo que a protección de menores se refiere. Los once puntos clave que contempla la legislación europea para proteger a la infancia, en TikTok, funcionan a favor de los pederastas. Es inadmisible.
Una sociedad como la española no puede permitir que los comportamientos más abyectos de la conducta humana tengan, gracias a una plataforma tecnológica, carta blanca en redes. Que TikTok les ponga el campo de juego. La plataforma se ha convertido, con su inacción, en un lugar en el que los pederastas se sienten como en casa. Impunes. Cómodos. Seguros. Si TikTok fuese una discoteca que está dejando entrar a menores y a pederastas en un mismo espacio, la autoridad competente intervendría de inmediato para que esto dejara de pasar. Pero el espacio digital no es un local que se puede clausurar y poner fin al problema, porque habrá plataformas nuevas a las que accederán los niños y seguro que también tratarán de acceder los pederastas. Lo que necesitamos es una aplicación eficiente de una legislación que ya existe: el Reglamento Europeo de Servicios Digitales y el Código Penal español.
Y, posiblemente, también legislación nueva. El parlamento que salga de las urnas el próximo 29 de noviembre tiene pendiente aprobar la Ley Orgánica para la protección de las personas menores de edad en los entornos digitales. Ojalá el amplio consenso que genera un tema tan sensible como este para millones de votantes haga que un pacto transversal lo logre antes de que acabe 2028, estableciendo mecanismos claros de responsabilidad penal y patrimonial para las grandes plataformas digitales que ignoren de forma sistemática y negligente las notificaciones de contenido ilegal de abuso sexual infantil.
También es crucial la habilitación de la Comisión Nacional de Mercados y Competencia, paralizada desde hace años, para que pueda cumplir las competencias que le encomienda el Reglamento de la UE de Servicios Digitales (DSA) y que son de vital importancia para la protección de los menores, como designar alertadores fiables de contenido ilegal o facilitar a los investigadores acceso a los datos de las plataformas para estudiar el fenómeno. Además, a nivel europeo, se está debatiendo el EU Kids Act: una pieza de legislación que puede establecer obligaciones específicas para plataformas como TikTok para evitar lo que hemos visto durante esta investigación.
Que algunas grandes empresas en este país hayan retirado sus inversiones publicitarias de TikTok da cuenta del amplio consenso que este tema genera en la sociedad. De lo que nos preocupa a todos que nuestra infancia esté expuesta, por la inacción de TikTok, a miles de pederastas de todo el mundo.

articles.title: 320 000 km et une batterie en pleine forme : cette étude de Ford réduit à néant la plus grande peur des automobilistes
articles.text:
Acheter une voiture électrique est aujourd’hui gage d’économies substantielles vu les prix du carburant. Mais nombreux sont ceux hésitant encore à franchir le pas en raison du manque de recul sur le vieillissement des batteries. Quand l’on entend ici et là qu’il faut parfois débourser des dizaines de milliers d’euros pour changer un pack défectueux, il y a effectivement de quoi angoisser. Pourtant, il n’y a vraiment pas lieu de s’inquiéter…
Ford a en ce sens mené une grande étude sur les Mustang Mach-E vendus aux États-Unis et au Canada. L’analyse a porté sur 36 000 modèles datant de 2021, avec un peu plus de 5 ans au compteur, donc. Et les résultats ne peuvent que rassurer. Car en moyenne, les exemplaires avaient parcouru 88 500 km en 5,2 ans tout en conservant près de 92 % de la capacité d’origine de leur batterie. La dégradation constatée n’est donc que de 8 %.
Perdre 40 km d’autonomie en 5 ans : drame ou miracle ?
Sur un rayon d’action théorique de 500 km, cela ne représente qu’une perte de 40 km d’autonomie. Notons au passage que les modèles impliqués dans l’étude sont tous équipés de batteries nickel manganèse cobalt dont la durée de vie est plus courte que celles dotées de la technologie lithium fer phosphate. Ce n’est qu’à partir de 2023 que Ford a décidé d’implémenter cette chimie à l’ensemble de ses Mustang Mach-E.
Les résultats devraient donc être encore meilleurs sur les modèles plus récents. Cela dit, ils demeurent déjà très satisfaisants sur les anciens packs nickel manganèse cobalt. D’ailleurs, plus de 2 000 exemplaires ayant plus de 160 000 km sont parvenus à maintenir la capacité de leurs batteries au-delà de 91 %. Mieux encore : après avoir dépassé les 320 000 km, 30 modèles gardaient encore 88 % de capacité de leur batterie.
Occasion : vers la fin de l’angoisse du remplacement de batterie ?
Il faut dire que Ford avait pris ses précautions pour ralentir le plus possible le vieillissement de ses accumulateurs. La marque testait physiquement les batteries en laboratoire afin d’essayer de prédire la dégradation des packs à l’aide de modèles informatiques. Kevin Vander Laan, responsable technique des cellules et des batteries haute tension chez Ford, admet que si ces prédictions sont importantes, la réalité reste le seul juge de paix.
« Nous voici aujourd’hui avec un bilan de cinq ans, et il est excellent », confirme-t-il. Bien sûr, les résultats varieront en fonction de l’usage du véhicule. Mais cela concorde presque avec les conclusions du cabinet Recurrent que nous vous avions partagées en mai dernier. Ces dernières indiquaient en effet que les véhicules électriques conservaient 95 % de leur autonomie d’origine après cinq ans.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.
Source : Inside EVs

articles.title: GTA 6 und PS5: So vermeidest du Controller-Ausfälle bei langen Sessions
articles.text:
GTA 6 auf der PS5: Warum Ladestationen für Dualsense-Controller jetzt unverzichtbar sind
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Nach mehr als einem Jahrzehnt Wartezeit erscheint am 19. November endlich GTA 6. Wer auf der Playstation 5 zockt, darf sich freuen, denn das Game nutzt die adaptiven Trigger und die haptische Vibration exzessiv – etwa beim Fahren über verschiedene Untergründe, bei Schießereien oder bei dynamischen Wettereffekten. Dadurch werden Hardware und Akku des Dualsense-Controllers allerdings stärker beansprucht als bei anderen Spielen. Wenn du in einer Session nahtlos den Controller wechseln möchtest, lohnt es sich, vor dem Release noch in eine Ladestation zu investieren. Hier erfährst du, worauf du beim Kauf achten solltest und mit welchen Kosten du rechnen musst.
Playstation 5: Warum sich eine Controller-Ladestation lohnt
GTA 6 lädt zu extrem langen Sessions ein. Gleichzeitig ist Rockstar Games dafür bekannt, die Grenzen der Technologie komplett auszureizen. Der Controller könnte deshalb deutlich kürzer durchhalten, als du es von anderen Spielen gewohnt bist. Um deinen Dualsense-Controller aufzuladen, hast du mehrere Optionen. Die Standardlösung ist das mitgelieferte USB-C-Kabel, das du mit einem der USB-Ports der Playstation 5 verbindest. So kannst du während des Ladens theoretisch weiterspielen, bist aber an die Kabellänge gebunden.
Auch deshalb lohnt sich eine separate Ladestation. Hier wird der Controller nicht über den USB-C-Port, sondern über die Metallkontakte an der Unterseite geladen. Das Click-in-Design funktioniert kinderleicht und lässt sich sogar mit einer Hand bedienen. Ladestationen bieten in der Regel Platz für zwei Controller gleichzeitig. Das ist ideal für den schnellen Wechsel, sodass du nahtlos weiterspielen kannst. Das Original von Sony und zertifizierte Drittanbieter bieten außerdem einen Überladungsschutz: Sie schalten den Strom automatisch ab, sobald der Akku voll ist. Das schont die Lebensdauer der Batterie.
So viel kostet eine Ladestation für deine PS5-Controller
Die gute Nachricht ist: Für eine Doppelladestation musst du nicht allzu tief in die Tasche greifen. Das Original von Sony ist bei Mediamarkt regulär für 34,99 Euro erhältlich. Aktuell ist es auf 26,99 Euro reduziert. Die weiße Dualsense-Ladestation lädt deine kabellosen Controller ebenso schnell wie eine direkte Verbindung mit der Playstation 5. So schonst du die Anschlüsse, ohne Leistung einzubüßen. Das vollständige Aufladen eines Controllers dauert typischerweise etwa zwei bis drei Stunden. Die Station verfügt über Gummifüße und ausreichend Gewicht, sodass sie nicht direkt abhebt, wenn du einen Controller herausnimmst.
Power A bietet eine Alternative, die preislich sogar noch attraktiver ist. Die offiziell für die Playstation 5 lizenzierte Ladestation hat ebenfalls zwei Steckplätze zum gleichzeitigen Aufladen von zwei kabellosen Controllern. Das Prinzip funktioniert wie beim Original: Du klickst den Controller nach unten ein, sodass die LED-Basis aufleuchtet und den Ladezustand anzeigt. Nach dem Aufladen klickst du erneut nach unten, um den Kontakt freizugeben und das Spiel zu starten. Käufer:innen schätzen die einfache Bedienung und die gute Passgenauigkeit. Die schwarz-weiße Ladestation ist bei Amazon schon für 19,99 Euro erhältlich.
Neben den beiden genannten Ladestationen gibt es zahlreiche weitere Modelle mit ähnlichem Design und Funktionen. Die Kosten starten hier bei etwa 15 Euro. Um Schäden am Controller zu vermeiden, lohnt es sich allerdings, direkt in die Original-Ladestation von Sony oder eine lizenzierte Alternative zu investieren – zumal die Preisunterschiede nicht groß sind. Die offiziell von Sony beworbenen Ladestationen schützen die empfindlichen Ladekontakte am besten und bieten ein intelligentes Lademanagement. Bei einem Blockbuster wie GTA 6 bist du damit ideal ausgestattet und kannst nahtlos weiterzocken, wenn ein Controller schlappmacht.

articles.title: TSMC employee data breach linked to cloud provider
articles.text:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) confirmed that personal employee data has been leaked online after a threat actor put 6.9GB of information allegedly stolen from the company up for auction.
The technology giant said the incident affected current and former employees but doesn’t impact its operations or customers.
The company verified the leaked information and confirmed that it matched "data stored in the system services of a cloud service provider," indicating an external breach.
TSMC is the world’s largest contract chipmaker, manufacturing advanced processors and other semiconductors for companies such as Apple and Nvidia.
Last year, it shipped approximately 15 million 12-inch-equivalent wafers and generated $122.4 billion in annual revenue.
TSMC's investigation found that the leaked information matched data stored in a cloud service provider it uses, pointing to a breach outside its own infrastructure.
The company is now notifying impacted staff and providing the necessary support, while also engaging a third-party cybersecurity firm to help manage the situation.
“TSMC has found that some of our current and former employee data was made available on an external website without authorization,” TSMC says in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
“Currently, we have found no evidence that TSMC’s systems have been compromised,” the company added.
Threat actor auctions the data
On November 8, someone using the alias ‘SmithBianl’ leaked on a hacker forum a text file containing 499 rows of information allegedly stolen from TSMC. The actor claimed the file was a sample of a 6.9GB dataset containing 46,000 employee records.
According to the post, the leaked information included TSMC employees' national ID numbers, addresses, contact details, and banking information.
SmithBianl offered the data for auction, with bidding starting at 3 BTC (approximately $65,000).
In the absence of a buyer, they warned that the data would be leaked for free in one week, setting the first deadline to November 15.
BleepingComputer has contacted TSMC to ask whether they have engaged with the threat actor and whether they planned to pay the hackers to prevent a full public leak of their employees’ data.
A spokesperson declined to comment at this stage.

articles.title: TE Connectivity at OCP Summit 2026 The Interview
articles.text:
At the 2026 OCP Global Summit, I had the chance to sit down with Brian Payne, Vice President of Product Management for the Digital Data Networks (DDN) business at TE Connectivity. Many of our readers will know Brian from his 26 years at Dell, but he had been at TE Connectivity for about a month when we spoke. TE’s booth was built around three interconnected system-level racks, an optical interconnect rack, a sidecar power rack, and a copper IT rack, so we walked through the high-speed connectivity, the power delivery, and why TE thinks its system-level approach matters as AI infrastructure scales. We previously published a short booth tour video on STHLabs that got a surprising amount of attention, so we figured we would follow it up with the interview we did while we were there.
As always, we lightly edited this for readability.
Brian Payne and TE Connectivity at OCP
Patrick Kennedy: Brian, could you tell us a little bit about yourself?
Brian Payne: Sure. First of all, thanks. It’s great to see you again. I am vice president of product management here at TE Connectivity. I’ve got a long history in this industry. I spent 26 years at Dell.
Patrick Kennedy: Could you give us a little bit of background about TE Connectivity?
Brian Payne: TE Connectivity is a very large organization that manufactures and provides connectivity across multiple industries. But one of the most exciting things we’re doing right now is in what we call DDN, our Digital Data Networks division. We have experienced massive growth over the last three years, all building out the AI infrastructure that’s powering everything we’re doing today. It’s an exciting space to be in, with tremendous upside ahead of us.
Patrick Kennedy: As part of that, TE Connectivity is well known for its contributions to OCP.
Brian Payne: TE Connectivity has been a part of OCP since 2017, so very early days. And as you can imagine, look around us. OCP has just boomed in terms of growth. TE Connectivity is focused on power and connectivity across all domains in the AI infrastructure. We have made tremendous contributions, and there are some exciting ones we’re going to talk about today.
448G and Next-Generation Front-Panel Connectivity
Patrick Kennedy: You have some things in your hand that I think you are super excited about. Could you tell us what these are and show us a little bit?
Brian Payne: Absolutely. At TE Connectivity, we’re thinking about how we deliver power for the data center and how we connect it. With every chip innovation, more and more bandwidth is coming. How do you get that out of the compute tray, and how do you get it into the network? One of the challenges is getting to 448. There are a lot of thermal challenges and signal integrity challenges to balance, and there’s a push in the industry to find the right solution. I would say there are two competing models out there. There’s XPO, which is a large.
Patrick Kennedy: And just to be clear here, these are 3D-printed models.
Brian Payne: The reason I’ve got a 3D-printed model is that just Monday of this week (at the October 2026 OCP Summit), in a partnership with NVIDIA and Cisco, we announced our new standard for getting to 448. That’s what I have in my hand right here. You will see that it’s a similar form factor to QSFP today. One of the things we’re trying to do is balance signal integrity, power delivery, and form factor, and not over-index on one or the other. We believe we have a winner.
When you talk about developing concepts, that’s exactly what we have here. The transceiver slides in, and we’ve got a unique way to compress it so that power delivery and signal integrity are handled separately. So our signal integrity is really, really strong. The design is also made so that, as we see the power of the transceiver escalate, we’ll be able to do cold plate liquid cooling to pull heat out of the system.
Patrick Kennedy: When you say 448G, you’re talking about the SerDes and really the per-lane communication speed.
Brian Payne: Absolutely.
Patrick Kennedy: That’s a big deal when we start talking about things like picojoules per bit, or how much power it takes to move data. But there are also a number of enabling technologies beyond USFP that you have behind us. Maybe we should start with some of the copper over here.
Copper Backplanes and Midplanes
Brian Payne: One of the huge areas of breakthrough in the industry has been copper backplane technology, and a combination of copper backplanes as well as midplanes. What we have here is an example of a midplane design, where a compute sled slides in along with power delivery. By going with this midplane design, you’re able to separate compute from GPU and then easily connect those together through the midplane. Then on the back side, we’ve got copper backplanes. In terms of an unlock for these rack-scale solutions, it is a highly technical, highly engineered solution that we have to produce in massive volumes.
TE is one of the only companies in the industry that’s able to do that. There are very few in the market, and we’re excited about that. We are focused from the chip all the way to the switch. We’ve got innovation in near-chip packaging. We’ve got innovation around optics. We’re thinking about front and back I/O connectivity and the cabling in between. We’ve got innovation and products across all of those that are being deployed today at massive scale.
Patrick Kennedy: One of the interesting things in AI deployments is just how many lanes of communication are happening in every single box in a rack. How do you make that, number one, not use too much power and not create too much heat, but then also make it reliable? I imagine that’s a lot of what TE Connectivity needs to work on.
Brian Payne: One of the things I’ve discovered, and it’s been a pleasant surprise coming into TE Connectivity, is the R&D on the front end. How do we get through the material science challenges and develop the parts necessary to unlock these massive increases in bandwidth, and then deal with all of the power that’s required to push these chips and push the data across the network?
Optics and Co-Packaged Optics
Patrick Kennedy: There are a number of technologies today focused on extending the usefulness of copper, but the next generation is really optics. I think you have a demo of that over here.
Brian Payne: The main thing I would say here is that you can go back to 10 Gigabit Ethernet, when we said the end of copper was coming, and copper is still prevalent in the industry. That being said, optics is there and solving a very, very important challenge. This is part of how we’re pathfinding and investing ahead. Earlier this year, we acquired an optics company, RAM Photonics. We’re bringing that into the product portfolio, and we’re massively investing in optics, from co-packaged optics as well as co-packaged copper, to getting the optics out of the system. So we’ve got a number of investments and new capabilities emerging to support that.
Patrick Kennedy: Folks have been talking about co-packaged optics in the industry for what feels like forever. What’s different about what’s happening today versus 10 years ago, when folks were saying, “Oh, we need co-packaged optics immediately”?
Brian Payne: I think it is the physics challenge, and how far you can route copper as we increase the number of lanes that are necessary. There is a point in time where we will have to make the pivot. I realize you could have said that 10 or 12 years ago, but it’s becoming more and more real as we face these challenges. That’s why our investment and productization are picking up in that space. But it’s not stopping our investment in copper, because copper is still the state of the art. It’s still important to deliver the outcomes our customers expect. That’s where we’ve got a dual investment.
Patrick Kennedy: One of the things you’re showing in the booth is some of the innovation around co-packaged optics, with connectors that go into the chip package so that you can service them. That was something folks didn’t know how to do even five or six years ago, and it’s a new innovation to bring co-packaged optics to the mass market and actually deploy it.
Brian Payne: When these are deployed at scale, it’s not just about getting the signal across the line. It’s about how you think about the system-level design and the operation, and what this looks like at scale. So to your point, serviceability is a critical design vector that drives innovation. That’s part of the TE approach: how do we not just get the technology working, but do it in a way that will support the massive volumes this industry is driving?
Power: The Sidecar Power Rack and Horizontal Busbar
Patrick Kennedy: This is a power shelf and a power rack. Why do we have a power rack, with racks focused on data connectivity on either side?
Brian Payne: To deliver the performance the industry is driving for, a massive amount of power is required to power the chips, and then to power the switches that connect them together. We simply don’t have the power density today to fit all of that in one rack, and that led to the innovation we see today. We’re starting to see sidecar designs like what we have here, which is a full rack of power distribution and cooling capabilities on one side.
Then on the back side, when we get around there, we’ve actually got a busbar that runs horizontally, which is unique in the industry. Nobody’s done that. We did it to solve a problem with one of our large customers, and to deliver power to the next rack, the IT rack, with the IT equipment, the compute sleds, and the switches. That’s a great example of us thinking whip to chip. How do we put together a practical solution that addresses the ever-growing thirst for more and more power?
Patrick Kennedy: One of the really interesting things there is that the density challenge is actually in the nodes, so that you can get the copper connectivity within a rack. It’s actually using power to solve a connectivity challenge. And one of the big innovations is moving that power out of the rack and figuring out how to get a lot of current back into it.
Brian Payne: Right. In this industry, we have talked about power constraints and half-full racks for years and years. We’ve talked about busbars, and none of that really took hold until the AI boom. That’s what led to the innovation where we are delivering liquid-cooled busbars that span the rack to deliver power across without having to amp up the current and the overall heat dissipation. It’s about finding that balance in power delivery, but doing it in an efficient way.
The next frontier is high voltage. We’ve got pathfinding concepts on the back side here where we’re pushing towards 800 volt. That’s what’s going to be necessary to get to a megawatt of power at the rack level. So how do we solve practically for the limitations of today, and also prepare ourselves for the future?
800V and Rack-to-Rack Power
Patrick Kennedy: One of the cool things about 800 volt is that it provides a more efficient power distribution path, which means your data center is more efficient. But there are cool things you’re doing as well. That 800 volt busbar back there has liquid cooling.
Brian Payne: Absolutely. And there are even things we can’t show you yet. Getting to 800 volt, number one, we’re thinking about how you get 800 volt all the way from the source. Every conversion has losses associated with it. So how do we bring it from the busways down into the rack, and then deliver it efficiently across the rack? To run this efficiently, liquid cooling to pull heat out is a critical element, and it’s something we’ve solved and have deployed across the industry.
Patrick Kennedy: You have another solution, which is a big, giant rack-to-rack cable. Can you tell me a little bit about that?
Brian Payne: Part of the issue is that once you get the power down to the IT equipment and you need to span multiple racks, you have to have an efficient way to get it rack to rack if a horizontal busbar isn’t the optimal choice. That’s why we’ve got prototype rack-to-rack 800 volt cables on the back of the system.
Patrick Kennedy: And that prototype is another example of how TE Connectivity is doing pathfinding with the OCP community and with customers to figure out how to solve these practical challenges.
Brian Payne: Our customer engagement starts in our customers’ data centers and in their offices, but also at places like OCP, where you can see we’re just covered up with people coming by. That inspires thought, new ideas, and future innovation. It’s super important to be a part of this community, to get those ideas in, show people what we’re thinking, and then iterate and evolve the designs going forward.
Pathfinding and Manufacturing at Scale
Patrick Kennedy: Could you give us some sense of how TE Connectivity doesn’t just make products for standards, but actually contributes to the pathfinding behind a lot of what is used in OCP?
Brian Payne: Absolutely. I’ll take power as an example. We think whip to chip. We’re one of the few, if not the only, company focused on the entire power delivery of the AI infrastructure at the AI rack. That means we see the bottlenecks before they occur, and we’re able to project ahead. The industry has the ambition to get to a megawatt of power at the rack level, and that has a lot of hard challenges. Behind us here, you’ll see some of the concepts we’re working on for how we’re going to deliver power rack to rack in the future. We get feedback on those from customers in real time, and we’re able to course correct and be ready when the industry needs us to go to full mass production.
Patrick Kennedy: I would imagine there are a bunch of steps that go into that. It starts with what problem you’re trying to solve. But then there’s also how you make something manufacturable, that you can build for a large AI data center and for an entire industry that’s really building around OCP.
Brian Payne: Everything starts with the customer. We’re partnering with the entire ecosystem, but especially the hyperscalers building out these AI data centers at a breakneck pace. The chip cycle, everything has moved faster, and we’ve got to be way ahead of where things are going: partnering, figuring out the problems they need to solve, innovating, delivering concepts, getting feedback, and continuing to iterate until we have the design the customers need.
Then that’s when we’ve got to shift to, “Oh my gosh, there are thousands of units to build to roll out in mass production.” We’ve got global manufacturing capabilities, and we’re able to rise up and produce high-quality, mass-produced parts to power the AI infrastructure we all enjoy today. TE Connectivity has a large global manufacturing footprint. We have 10 manufacturing facilities around the world, from China to Southeast Asia to North America, all focused just on the DDN business to power what’s going on in this industry.
What Is Driving TE Connectivity
Patrick Kennedy: Brian, I’ve known you for years. At the end of the day, what are the big things that are driving you?
Brian Payne: It all starts with our customers. What do they need us to do? They need us to be at the forefront of technology innovation, and they need us to be able to deliver to support their business. That means we have to be able to design high-quality products that solve the technical challenges we have. But just as important, we’ve got to be able to manufacture at scale. We’ve got that balanced investment where we can do that across power and connectivity to push the industry forward.
Patrick Kennedy: Awesome.
Final Words
A big thank you to Brian for taking the time to walk us through TE Connectivity’s booth at OCP Summit 2026. The broader theme was that AI infrastructure is no longer just a chip problem.
Getting to 448G per lane, scaling copper while preparing for co-packaged optics, and moving rack power toward 800V and the megawatt-class rack all have to work together at the system level, and then be manufactured at scale.

articles.title: New Windows zero-day turns Microsoft's own security fix into a path to full system access
articles.text:
Facepalm: Last year, Microsoft started digitally signing the log files of a Windows component that attackers had been abusing for years. The idea was that any tampered log would simply get rejected. But that same safeguard is now the way in for a new zero-day that lets a standard user take complete control of a PC. Ironically, the attack needs Microsoft's own antivirus running to pull it off.
This latest exploit is called SignDrop. It comes from Abdelhamid Naceri, a former Microsoft employee who has been dumping unpatched Windows bugs online under the name Nightmare Eclipse since April. He published the code on GitHub on Tuesday, just as Microsoft was rolling out its November security updates.
A bug like this is notable because it can turn a minor infection into a full takeover. Malware that slips in through a shady download usually runs with the same limited rights as the user. SignDrop would let it climb to the very top, where it can switch off security tools and dig in for good. And since the code is public, anyone can try it.
The bug sits in the Common Log File System (CLFS), which apps and drivers across Windows use to keep their logs. The problem is a small companion file it creates next to each log to help with recovery. That file inherits its permissions from the log, so whoever set up the log gets control of it.
That's where Defender comes in, since it runs with the highest privileges on the PC. SignDrop tricks the antivirus into opening a log the attacker prepared ahead of time. So the companion file gets created with Defender's top-level rights, yet the attacker still gets to control it.
From there, it's a short hop to a command prompt running as SYSTEM. That's the built-in account Windows reserves for its own core processes. It has more say over the PC than even an admin account.
Outside testing paints a much narrower picture. Vulnerability analyst Will Dormann told Ars Technica he managed to reproduce the exploit, but only on PCs running this year's Windows 11 26H2 update. Those machines also need to have been set up for more than 90 days, so a freshly installed copy won't work. Out of all the machines Dormann has on hand, exactly one qualifies.
For its part, Microsoft says it's investigating and hasn't seen the flaw exploited in the wild. The company also claims Defender already detects and blocks the attack.
Even so, Naceri's track record makes SignDrop hard to wave off. Three of his earlier Defender exploits, including BlueHammer, ended up in real attacks after he released them. As for a fix, one likely won't arrive before December's Patch Tuesday on the 8th unless Microsoft rushes it out.

articles.title: Papelera de WhatsApp: qué es, dónde está y para qué sirve
articles.text:
La papelera de WhatsApp no es una carpeta donde se guarden temporalmente los archivos eliminados. En realidad, la aplicación de Meta cuenta con un administrador de almacenamiento que permite identificar fotografías, videos, audios y documentos que ocupan memoria en el celular.
WhatsApp permite revisar el contenido multimedia que más espacio consume, incluidos los archivos reenviados muchas veces y el material descargado desde los canales.
Desde esa herramienta, cada usuario puede seleccionar qué conservar y qué eliminar sin borrar conversaciones completas.
Antes de eliminar contenido, conviene comprobar que no se trate de documentos, fotografías o videos importantes. Algunos archivos pueden descargarse otra vez desde el chat, pero otros podrían no estar disponibles si fueron borrados de la conversación o de los servidores de Meta.
Dónde está la papelera de WhatsApp
Lo que suele identificarse como la papelera es el administrador de almacenamiento. Esta función permite localizar fotografías, videos y otros documentos que ocupan espacio en el dispositivo.
Para acceder a los archivos reenviados muchas veces, hay que ingresar en Ajustes, seleccionar Almacenamiento y datos y después Administrar almacenamiento.
Para qué sirve la papelera de WhatsApp
El administrador de almacenamiento sirve para localizar contenido que puede haberse acumulado con el tiempo.
Entre los archivos que suelen ocupar más memoria están los videos de gran tamaño, las imágenes reenviadas repetidamente, los audios y el contenido multimedia de los canales.
La herramienta organiza los elementos según el espacio que ocupan o la cantidad de veces que fueron reenviados. Esto permite detectar memes, fotografías o videos que circulan en distintos chats y grupos y que pueden duplicar el consumo de memoria.
Permite revisar los archivos de más de cinco megabytes, una categoría que suele incluir videos largos y fotografías de alta resolución. De esta manera, es posible liberar espacio sin tener que revisar cada conversación de forma individual.
De qué otras formas ahorrar espacio en WhatsApp
Una alternativa es borrar la memoria caché de WhatsApp. Estos son archivos temporales que la aplicación guarda para facilitar su funcionamiento y acelerar algunas tareas.
En Android, esta opción se encuentra en la configuración del celular. Los nombres de los apartados pueden variar según la marca y la versión del sistema operativo, por lo que es importante no confundir “Borrar caché” con “Borrar datos” o “Borrar almacenamiento”, opciones que pueden eliminar información de la aplicación y requerir una nueva configuración.
Los canales de WhatsApp también pueden consumir memoria, ya que las fotografías, GIF y videos consultados pueden descargarse en el dispositivo.
El administrador de almacenamiento permite eliminar esos archivos sin dejar de seguir los canales, aunque será necesario descargarlos de nuevo si se quiere volver a consultar una publicación cuyo contenido ya fue borrado.
Director de WhatsApp habla sobre el futuro de la plataforma
Kunal Shah, director global de WhatsApp, anticipó que el futuro de la aplicación combinará una experiencia más sencilla con servicios para resolver tareas desde el chat.
El ejecutivo planteó que la plataforma busca mantener conectadas a las personas y reducir pasos para realizar gestiones.
Su plan se apoya en tres ejes: mejorar la comunicación, incorporar opciones de pago de cuentas y préstamos, y usar inteligencia artificial para ahorrar tiempo. Shah sostuvo que actividades comienzan en una conversación y obligan a salir de la aplicación.
WhatsApp trabaja con socios de los sectores financiero y de telecomunicaciones, aunque no informó nombres ni fechas para funciones.
La privacidad seguirá siendo central, según Shah. Los mensajes y las llamadas conservarán el cifrado de extremo a extremo. WhatsApp ofrece un asistente de inteligencia artificial para resumir mensajes y redactar borradores.
Cada día, los usuarios envían más de 10.000 millones de mensajes de voz y 4.000 millones de stickers, de acuerdo con la compañía.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. Maier, R. Spachtholz, K. Glöckl, C. M. Bustamante, S. Lingl, M. Maczejka, J. Schön, A. Riedel, K. Richter, F. J. Giessibl, F. P. Bonafé, M. A. Huber, A. Rubio, J. Repp, R. Huber. Tracking electrons at the space-time limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (8): 961 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01932-0

articles.title: Quase R$ 5 milhões: Claro vai fornecer iPhones e mais celulares para Senado • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Quase R$ 5 milhões: Claro vai fornecer iPhones e mais celulares para Senado
Acordo custará R$ 4,96 milhões e garante serviços de telefonia da operadora para o Senado Federal. Parlamentares recebem um iPhone 18 Pro cada a partir de janeiro.
A Claro venceu a licitação de fornecimento de celulares e serviços de telefonia móvel para senadores e demais servidores do parlamento (Pregão 290/2026). O custo estimado é de R$ 4,96 milhões, destinados para a oferta de 425 celulares e planos para ligações e dados móveis.
Dessa forma, a partir de janeiro de 2027 cada senador será contemplado com um iPhone 18 Pro, enquanto outros 330 servidores receberão dispositivos Android, como Samsung Galaxy A37 5G e Moto G86 5G. Além disso, todos terão franquia de 50 GB para acesso à internet, entre outros serviços.
É importante ressaltar que os celulares serão cedidos em regime de comodato, ou seja, trata-se de um empréstimo por parte da Claro. Em 2029, os dispositivos serão substituídos por aparelhos mais novos. Caso o acordo siga valendo, o mesmo vale para 2031, assim por diante. As informações foram divulgadas pelo UOL.
A publicação da licitação gerou um burburinho no Senado e na Câmara dos Deputados, levando a críticas tanto de congressistas da base do governo quanto de oposição. Deputados como Tabata Amaral (PSB-SP) e Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG) foram contrários ao edital apresentado.
O senador Cleitinho (Republicanos-MG) chegou a criar uma consulta pública que recebeu mais de 33 mil votos a favor do veto à compra de iPhones pelo Senado. O presidente da Casa, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), respondeu a reação dos colegas e da sociedade, afirmando que o edital não trata da compra de celulares, e sim do empréstimo dos aparelhos.
A proposta do edital é substituir um contrato de 2022 que garantiu 93 iPhones 13 Pro para senadores e diretores, além de 290 outros dispositivos intermediários a demais servidores. O novo pregão, vencido pela Claro, prevê o empréstimo de modelos mais avançados aos parlamentares, além da troca de aparelhos a cada dois anos.
A operadora será responsável pelos iPhones 18 Pro e demais dispositivos fornecidos ao Senado, além de oferecer serviços de ligação e dados móveis para a Casa. O orçamento previsto no pregão era de aproximadamente R$ 6 milhões, mas a proposta da Claro dá conta de R$ 4.957.905,60.
O acordo passa a valer em 1º de janeiro de 2027, caso aprovado. O Senado ainda precisa homologar a decisão para dar continuidade no serviço contratado.

articles.title: LG’s budget-friendly B6E OLED TV is up to 50 percent off this weekend
articles.text:
LG’s B6E was already one of the most affordable OLED TVs you could buy, but it’s an even better deal now that it’s included as part of Best Buy’s latest doorbuster event. Now through the end of today, November 15th, the 55-inch model is 50 percent off, dropping it to an all-time low of $699.99 ($700 off) at Best Buy. If you want a larger 4K set, the 65- and 77-inch models are also discounted, dropping them to $999.99 ($900 off) and $1,499.99 ($1,200 off), respectively.
LG’s budget-friendly B6E OLED TV is up to 50 percent off this weekend
The excellent OLED offers great contrast and plenty of gamer-ready features at a fraction of the cost.
Although it’s not as bright as LG’s pricier C6, the B6E still delivers the excellent contrast and deep blacks OLEDs are often praised for. It’s nearly identical to the standard B6, except it comes with a simpler remote that lacks the motion controls and voice features found on LG’s Magic Remote. It supports Dolby Vision and HDR10 for more lifelike colors and detail in bright and dark scenes, along with Dolby Atmos for more immersive audio. And with Apple AirPlay and Google Cast built in, you can easily stream content from your phone or tablet and access a variety of streaming apps, including Netflix, HBO Max, and YouTube via LG’s webOS platform.
The B6 also offers a lot of features gamers will appreciate. It has a 120Hz refresh rate for modern gaming consoles, which is still plenty fast even if it doesn’t rival the 165Hz refresh rate on the C6. It also offers variable refresh rate support — including Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium — to help minimize screen tearing. You also get a zippy Alpha 8 Gen 3 AI processor and four HDMI 2.1 ports, making it easy to connect multiple consoles. It may lack some of the more advanced features found on LG’s more premium OLED TVs, but at 50 percent off, the B6 is a great option if you want the benefits of OLED without spending a fortune.

articles.title: Google : l'IA capte tant de recherches que des annonceurs n'arrivent plus à dépenser leur budget
articles.text:
Deux semaines après une chute de plus de 12 % en Bourse, qui avait effacé environ 500 milliards de dollars de capitalisation, Alphabet voit le malaise gagner le cœur de son réacteur, la publicité. Un annonceur américain, client depuis sept ans, ne parviendrait plus à écouler son budget quotidien d’environ 2 000 dollars, faute de vues et de clics à acheter. Il met en cause les assistants IA, qui répondent désormais à des questions qui passaient hier par une recherche classique. Six annonceurs et dirigeants d’agence auraient déjà basculé une partie de leurs budgets vers Meta.
Les acheteurs de pub passent leurs dépenses au crible
Dix-huit acheteurs média passent au crible entre 10 et 30 % des budgets de recherche confiés à Google. Certains se disent prêts à déplacer rapidement une partie de ces sommes vers d’autres canaux, Meta en tête, si les performances fléchissent. Le 2 novembre, le groupe a d’ailleurs déplacé les Aperçus IA vers la colonne de droite des résultats sur ordinateur, un emplacement moins central, pour les recherches de marque. Ces requêtes, qui portent le nom d’une entreprise ou d’un produit, comptent parmi les plus disputées de la régie, les annonceurs achetant souvent leur propre nom pour verrouiller le haut de page.
Au troisième trimestre, les revenus de la recherche ont pourtant encore progressé de 12 %, après 17 % au trimestre précédent. Les clics payants gagnent 8 % et le coût par clic 4 %, signe que la régie vend toujours plus d’espaces, un peu plus cher. Devant les analystes, le directeur commercial d’Alphabet, Philipp Schindler, a toutefois reconnu que le mode IA monétise moins bien que la recherche classique. C’est cet aveu, parmi d’autres déceptions du trimestre, que la Bourse avait sanctionné fin octobre.
Google conteste la lecture la plus sombre et assure que la majorité des requêtes posées au mode IA viendraient s’ajouter aux recherches classiques.
En France, un mode IA sans la moindre publicité
Lancé aux États-Unis au printemps 2025, le mode IA occupe un onglet dédié de la page de résultats et répond aux internautes français depuis le 22 juillet. Ses réponses n’affichent aucune annonce à ce jour. La monétisation se joue ailleurs. Depuis le 28 octobre, des publicités se glissent au fil des réponses du mode IA dans dix pays, pour l’essentiel anglophones. Le Royaume-Uni, le Brésil et le Mexique doivent suivre d’ici la fin de l’année.
Aucun pays de l’Union européenne ne figure sur la liste, et aucune date n’a été annoncée pour le marché européen. Les annonceurs français peuvent donc observer ce qui se joue outre-Atlantique, où leurs homologues découvrent des campagnes qui ne trouvent plus leur audience.
